title: N=4 super Yang–Mills in Costello’s formalism — Step 1

blocks.source: 1. Overview

This manuscript constructs the one-loop quantum Batalin–Vilkovisky theory of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, together with the transformations of its local operators under the whole superconformal algebra, in the renormalisation formalism of Costello [C07] and Costello–Gwilliam [CG2]. The single regulator is a lower cutoff $\varepsilon>0$ on Schwinger time; the upper end of every Schwinger integral is $\infty$, and no infrared scale and no dimensional continuation enter. This overview states what is constructed, where the construction needs care, how the chapters are organised, and the results of this first step.
1.1 What is constructed

The fields are those of ten-dimensional super Yang–Mills theory reduced to $\mathbb R^4$ [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], complexified. Write $V$ for the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$ and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for the six transverse directions, and $\mathfrak g$ for the complexified gauge Lie algebra with its invariant pairing $(-,-)$, which carries the coupling. The gauge field $A$ is a ten-component one-form with values in $\mathfrak g$: its components along $V$ form the connection $A|_V$, and its components $\iota_wA$, $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, are the six scalars. The gaugino $\lambda$ takes values in the ten-dimensional semi-spin representation $\Sigma$, which in four dimensions is $S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*$, with $S_\pm$ the two Weyl spinor representations and $W$ the four-dimensional R-symmetry space [ESW, §10]; spinors stay index free throughout. The ghost $c$ and the antifields $A^*$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$ complete the fields [ESW, Def 3.2, Rem 1.36]. The action $S$ is [ESW, (31)] reduced to four dimensions; its quadratic part defines the linear differential $Q$, the rest is the interaction $I$, and $\{-,-\}$ is the odd Poisson bracket [C07, Lemma 4.3.2].

Costello's construction needs three more objects. A gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$, here of Feynman type, makes $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ the Laplacian on every field. The heat kernel $K_t$ of $H$ at Schwinger time $t$ [C07, §6.5] gives the propagator
P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt ,
and Feynman graphs with these edges assemble into the renormalisation group flow of an even functional $J$,
W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J\big)=\hbar\log\Big(e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}\Big)\qquad[\text{CG2, §7.2.7}],

with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ the second-order operator contracting two fields with the kernel $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §6.4]; this is the functional called $\Gamma$ in [C07, Def 6.6.1]. As in Theorem B of [C07], the counterterm $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is the singular part of the graph expansion, extracted graph by graph, with coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ at one loop; it is local, and $W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big)$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$. A local operator $O$, for instance $\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ with $\omega$ a compactly supported four-form [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3], enters through a square-zero parameter $\delta$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.1]: the counterterm $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ of the family $I+\delta O$ defines the local operator at the UV end, $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and its quantum observable is
O[\infty]=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big)\qquad[\text{CG2, Def 8.3.1.3}].

The superconformal algebra $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ [SW, (7), (17)] acts through an equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, a Maurer–Cartan element of the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27] with differential $d_{CE}$. Building $O[\infty]$ from the equivariant interaction, the transformation of $O$ along a generator $x_1\in\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the component $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)$. Along the dilatation $\Delta$, the generator $2E$ of [SW, (17)] with $E$ the Euler vector field [SW, (3)], it is the anomalous dimension; along the supercharges $Q^i_\alpha$, $\bar Q_{\dot\alpha i}$ and the special supercharges $S^\alpha_i$, $\bar S^{\dot\alpha i}$ (the names of [SW, (8)]) it is the quantum-corrected supersymmetry; along the special conformal generators it is the primary condition. The program therefore has two outputs: the quantised interaction, with its counterterms and its quantum master equation, and, for every local operator, its observable and its transformations along all of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$.
1.2 Three points that need care

Operators. Inserting a composite operator produces divergences, and the limit defining $O[\infty]$ exists for many choices of the functional $O(\varepsilon)$. At scale $\infty$, however, $K_\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}K_t=0$ on $\mathbb R^4$, and $P(0,\infty)$ is a contracting homotopy for $Q$: for compactly supported $\alpha$,
Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha\big)+P(0,\infty)\star(Q\alpha)=\alpha ,

where $P(0,\infty)\star$ is the operator with kernel $P(0,\infty)$ [C07, §6.3]. Away from finitely many zero-mode classes, every $Q$-closed functional at scale $\infty$ without constant term is therefore $Q$-exact, and an arbitrary $O(\varepsilon)$ carries no cohomological information. The content of an operator is the locality of $O(\varepsilon)$: $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ with local coefficients in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$. Locality and the existence of the limit fix the singular part uniquely, and the finite part is the scheme. An equation $[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](x_1)=Y[\infty]$ has content because $Y$ is required to be local, and anomalous dimensions are classes in the cohomology of local functionals.

Counterterms. Theorem B fixes the singular part $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ uniquely. The cutoff on every edge breaks gauge invariance and superconformal symmetry, and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ contains $\varepsilon^{-1}$ mass terms with nonzero image under $Q$. The quantum master equation, transported to the UV boundary, then forces finite local counterterms. They are constrained by the master equation and fixed up to a choice; this choice is the renormalisation condition, part of the definition of the quantum theory and of every operator.
The UV boundary. The lower end $t=\varepsilon$ of the Schwinger integral carries two kernels,
\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon,\qquad (Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon,\qquad L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon ,

the second being [C07, Lemma 10.2.1] with $K_\infty=0$. Edges pinned at $t=\varepsilon$ and carrying $L_\varepsilon$ produce the singular coefficients and the scaling behaviour. Edges carrying $K_\varepsilon$ produce the defects of the quantum master equation and the transformations of observables, through

(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\big(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon\big),\qquad \Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}\quad[\text{C07, §10.1}].
Every singular or anomalous coefficient of this manuscript is carried by such boundary edges.
1.3 Plan of the chapters

Chapter 1 fixes the fields, the odd pairing, the reduced action with its linear differential and vertices, and the classical master equation. Chapter 2 realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ and constructs the equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ in the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex. Chapter 3 constructs the Feynman-gauge $Q^{GF}$, records which axioms of [C07, Def 4.3.3] it satisfies, and proves the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity at scale $\infty$ and the one-loop formula. Chapter 4 computes the one-loop counterterms of the action in the two-, three- and four-point sectors and the quantum master equation at the UV boundary. Chapter 5 computes $O(\varepsilon)$ for the single letters and the scalar bilinears, Chapter 6 their dilatation through the scaling covariance of the regulator, and Chapter 7 the selection rules for the other superconformal components and the program of Steps 2–5.
1.4 Results of Step 1
All one-loop coefficients are rational multiples of
\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)},
which is independent of $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ for simple $\mathfrak g$; below it is called the unit and written out in every formula.

• Chapter 2. The equivariant action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, with $S^{(k)}=0$ for $k\ge3$, satisfies its master equation for every $\mathfrak g$ on the Poincaré supersymmetry subalgebra, in arity $0$, in arity $3$ with at most one or with three odd arguments, and in every arity $\ge4$; the remaining components, of arities $1$ to $3$, hold for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ at sampled generators, with the probability bound stated there.
• Chapter 3. With the Feynman-gauge operator, $d^*d$ being the positive Laplacian,
H=[Q,Q^{GF}]=d^*d\otimes\mathrm{id},\qquad (Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon,\qquad (Q^{GF})^2\neq0 ;
conditions (1), (2), (4) of [C07, Def 4.3.3] hold and (3), (5) fail, and every identity used later rests on the conditions that hold.
• Chapter 4. The part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ quadratic in the fields is, with $\mathrm{dvol}$ the Euclidean volume form and ${\not d}$ the Dirac operator [ESW, §2.1],
• Chapter 4. Through the cubic and quartic sectors the $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is
\log\varepsilon\,\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\,\big(Q+\{I,-\}\big)\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(2(A,A^*)-4(\lambda^*,\lambda)-(c^*,c)\Big),

which multiplies the tree vertices $(A|_V)^3$, $A|_V(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $\lambda\lambda A|_V$, $\lambda\lambda A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, $cA|_VA^*|_V$, $cA|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, $c\lambda\lambda^*$, $ccc^*$, $(A|_V)^4$, $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^4$ by $6,6,10,10,1,1,1,1,8,8,8$ units; its component along the coupling vanishes, so the coupling is unrenormalised at one loop, and the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ terms lie in the quadratic sector.

• Chapter 4. In the sector $(c,A|_V)$ of the quantum master equation the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ parts cancel against $-Q$ of the mass counterterm, no $\log\varepsilon$ appears, and the finite obstruction is

-\frac{27}{8}\,\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)=\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\,Q\!\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V),
removed by the finite change $I\mapsto I-\frac{27}{16}\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$.

• Chapter 5. The single letters $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_wA)$, $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(A|_V))$, $\int\omega\,(\zeta,\lambda)$, $\int\omega\,(X,c)$, with fixed $X\in\mathfrak g$, $v\in V$, $\zeta\in\Sigma^*\otimes\mathfrak g$, have $O(\varepsilon)=O$. For $O=\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$, with $w$ running over an orthonormal basis of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$,

\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]=\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\log\varepsilon\Big[4\,O-2(w_1,w_2)\sum_w\int\omega\,(\iota_wA,\iota_wA)\Big]+\frac{2\hbar\dim\mathfrak g\,(w_1,w_2)}{16\pi^2\varepsilon}\int\omega ;
for $(w_1,w_2)=0$, where $O$ lies in the traceless part, and for the trace $\sum_w\int\omega\,(\iota_wA,\iota_wA)$ this gives

• Chapter 6. Let $O$ have Weyl weight $w_O$ (the sum of the weights $1$ of $A$, $\tfrac32$ of $\lambda$, $0$ of $c$, plus the number of derivatives), so that $\Delta=2E$ acts on it classically by $2(E+w_O)$, $E$ acting on its density. The scaling covariance of the regulator, together with the identification of the Weyl scaling with the dilatation cochain that Chapter 6 states as the task of Step 2, gives
[(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]](\Delta)=2\Big(E+w_O+\text{coefficient}\cdot\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\Big)O[\infty]+\cdots,

the dots being terms built from $(Q+\{I,-\})O$, and the coefficient given in the table. In the normalisation $\Delta=-E$ of [SW, (3)] the same statement reads $-\big(E+w_O+\text{coefficient}\cdot\text{unit}\big)O[\infty]+\cdots$.

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(N)$ with $(X,Y)=-\frac{4\hbar}{g^2}\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, $\operatorname{tr}$ the trace in the defining representation and $g$ the Yang–Mills coupling (Chapter 6), the unit equals $-g^2N/(32\pi^2)$, and $-24$ units equal $3g^2N/(4\pi^2)$, the one-loop anomalous dimension of the Konishi operator; this serves as a consistency check.

• Chapter 7. Translations, rotations and the R-symmetry commute with $Q^{GF}$ and $H$; their components can be chosen with no one-loop correction, and the counterterms of the traceless and the trace scalar bilinears stay in their own representations. Along the supercharges, the special supercharges and the special conformal generators the regulator moves, and the one-loop output lies in an explicit list of local structures; for the traceless scalar bilinear the supercharge component is a multiple of its classical structure.
2. The classical theory

Every number computed in Step 1 is a coefficient in front of a local functional, and its sign and normalisation are inherited from three classical data: the odd pairing on the fields, the BV action and the linear differential $Q$. The sources supply the ten-dimensional action [ESW, (31)] and its dimensional reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20, §10.3], while the pairing on the antifields stays implicit in the phrase "natural $(-1)$-shifted symplectic structure" [ESW, Def 1.34]. This chapter fixes all three data for the reduction to Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, writes the interaction vertex by vertex, and shows that the classical master equation determines the relative signs of the pairing.
2.1 Spaces and the dimensional reduction
Definition 2.1 (Spaces).
• $V_{10}$ is the ten-dimensional complexified Euclidean space of [ESW, (31)], with its nondegenerate symmetric form $(-,-)$, and
V_{10}=V\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp ,

where $V$ is the complexification of $\mathbb R^4$ (the directions of spacetime) and $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ consists of the six transverse directions. In the notation of [ESW, §2.6] the ten-dimensional space is $V_{\mathbb R}$ and the four-dimensional subspace is $W_{\mathbb R}$; here $W$ alone denotes the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10].

• $\mathfrak g$ is the complexified gauge Lie algebra, with bracket $[-,-]$ and a nondegenerate invariant symmetric pairing $(-,-)$, positive definite on the compact real form [ESW, §3.1]. The coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$. The inverse pairing is the element $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$.

• $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^*$ are the two sixteen-dimensional semi-spin representations of $\mathfrak{so}(V_{10})$, forming the $\mathbb Z/2$-graded Clifford module $\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*$ with Clifford action $\rho$ and pairing $(-,-)\colon\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ [ESW, §2.1]:
\rho(v_1)\rho(v_2)+\rho(v_2)\rho(v_1)=2(v_1,v_2),\qquad (\rho(v)Q_1,Q_2)=(Q_1,\rho(v)Q_2),\qquad v,v_1,v_2\in V_{10}.
• $\Gamma$ is the $\Gamma$-pairing $\Gamma\colon\mathrm{Sym}^2(\Sigma)\to V_{10}$, $\Gamma\colon\mathrm{Sym}^2(\Sigma^*)\to V_{10}$ [ESW, (28)]:

• $q\colon\wedge^\bullet V_{10}\to\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$ is antisymmetrisation, $q(v_1\wedge v_2)=v_1v_2-(v_1,v_2)$ [ESW, (29)]. Applied to a two-form, such as $F_A$, the symbol $\rho$ means $\rho\circ q$, as in $\rho(F_A)$ [ESW, (33)].

• $d$ is the exterior derivative along $\mathbb R^4$; every field is constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The operator $d^*$ is the formal adjoint of $d$ for the Euclidean metric, $\mathrm{dvol}$ is the Euclidean volume form of $\mathbb R^4$, and ${\not d}=\rho\circ d$ is the Dirac operator $\Gamma(\Sigma)\to\Gamma(\Sigma^*)$ [ESW, §2.1]; the same formula on $\Sigma^*$-valued functions is written ${\not d}|_{\Sigma^*}$.
The four-dimensional content of $\Sigma$ is [ESW, §10, §10.3]
\Sigma\cong S_+\otimes W\oplus S_-\otimes W^*,\qquad \dim W=4,\qquad W\cong S_+^6\ \text{as a representation of}\ \mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)\cong SL(4,\mathbb C),
with $S_\pm$ the two-dimensional semi-spin representations of $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$.
Proposition 2.2 (Four-dimensional chirality).

Fix an orientation of $V$ and let $\mathrm{dvol}$ also denote the corresponding four-form on $V$. Then $\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))$ squares to $1$ on $\Sigma$ and on $\Sigma^*$, with eigenvalues $+1$ and $-1$ each of multiplicity $8$. Writing
one has, for $v\in V$ and $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$,
\rho(v)\colon S_+\otimes W\to S_-\otimes W,\qquad \rho(w)\colon S_+\otimes W\to S_+\otimes W^*,
and correspondingly on the other summands: $\rho(v)$ exchanges the four-dimensional chiralities and $\rho(w)$ preserves them.
Proof.

Let $v_1,\dots,v_4$ be an oriented orthonormal basis of $V$, so $q(\mathrm{dvol})=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ in $\mathrm{Cl}(V_{10})$. By the Clifford relation the $v_i$ anticommute pairwise and square to $1$, hence

For $v=v_1$, moving $v_1$ through $v_1v_2v_3v_4$ meets $v_2,v_3,v_4$ once each, so $v_1\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1$; the same holds for every $v\in V$ by linearity. For $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, $w$ anticommutes with all four $v_i$, so $w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=(+1)(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,w$. Since $\rho(v)$ maps $\Sigma\to\Sigma^*$, the first relation reads $\rho(v)\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))|_{\Sigma}=-\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))|_{\Sigma^*}\rho(v)$, so $\rho(v)$ maps the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $-1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$; the second relation gives $\rho(w)$ mapping the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma$ to the $+1$ eigenspace on $\Sigma^*$. For the multiplicities, pick a unit vector $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$. The even element $v_1w$ satisfies $(v_1w)^2=-v_1^2w^2=-1$ and $v_1w\,(v_1v_2v_3v_4)=-(v_1v_2v_3v_4)\,v_1w$, so $\rho(v_1w)$ is an invertible endomorphism of $\Sigma$ (and of $\Sigma^*$) exchanging the two eigenspaces of $\rho(q(\mathrm{dvol}))$; hence each eigenspace has dimension $16/2=8$. ∎
Remark 2.3.

The names of the eigenspaces depend on the orientation of $V$; the opposite orientation exchanges $S_+\leftrightarrow S_-$ in all four of them. This choice is a convention of the program, fixed once and used in Chapter 2 to name the supercharges.
2.2 Fields, degrees and parities
Definition 2.4 (Fields).
The BRST fields of [ESW, Def 3.2], reduced along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56, Prop 2.20], form
F_{\rm gauge}=\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;\mathfrak g[1])\oplus\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;V_{10}^\vee\otimes\mathfrak g)\oplus\Omega^0(\mathbb R^4;\Pi\Sigma\otimes\mathfrak g),
with sections $(c,A,\lambda)$. The space of BV fields is [ESW, Rem 1.36]
\mathscr E=F_{\rm gauge}\oplus F_{\rm gauge}^![-1],

with antifields $(c^*,A^*,\lambda^*)$; duals are identified through $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$, the metric of $V_{10}$, the pairing $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ and $\mathrm{dvol}$. The component of $A$ along $V$ is the connection $A|_V$, the component along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ is $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, and $\iota_wA=A(w)$ for $w\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ are the six scalars. We write $\mathscr E_c$ for the compactly supported elements of $\mathscr E$.

The degrees are those of [ESW, Rem 1.33]: the ghost $c$ is a section in degree $-1$, which forces $A^*$ in degree $+1$ and $c^*$ in degree $+2$. Signs follow the Koszul rule for the total parity, the sum of the $\mathbb Z$-degree and the $\mathbb Z/2$-degree modulo $2$ [ESW, §1.1].

2.3 Pairing and bracket
Definition 2.5 (Odd pairing).

The odd pairing $\langle\,,\rangle$ on $\mathscr E$ [C07, Def 4.3.1; ESW, Def 1.13, Def 1.16] is nonzero exactly between a field and its antifield. For each of the three pairs, call the member of even total parity the even member: $A$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$; their partners $A^*$, $\lambda$, $c$ are odd. For a section $e_0$ in the slot of an even member and a section $e_1$ in the slot of its partner,
\langle e_0,e_1\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1),\qquad \langle e_1,e_0\rangle=-\langle e_0,e_1\rangle ,

where $(e_0,e_1)$ is the fibre pairing of Definition [2.4](#b-00081); for the pair $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ it is $(e_1,e_0)$ with $(-,-)\colon\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*\to\mathbb C$ tensored with $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$.
Definition 2.6 (Bracket and the kernel of the identity).
The kernel $K_0$ of the identity [C07, §10.1] has nonzero components exactly in the slot pairs
A\otimes A^*,\quad A^*\otimes A,\quad \lambda^*\otimes\lambda,\quad \lambda\otimes\lambda^*,\quad c^*\otimes c,\quad c\otimes c^*,

each equal to $-\delta(x-y)$ times the inverse of the fibre pairing: $(-,-)^{-1}$ tensored with the inverse metric of $V_{10}$ for $A$, $A^*$, with the canonical element of $\Sigma\otimes\Sigma^*$ for $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and with $1$ for $c$, $c^*$; here $x,y\in\mathbb R^4$ are the two positions. The bracket is the odd Poisson bracket of [C07, Lemma 4.3.2], defined for $f$ local and $g$ arbitrary, given by
\{f,g\}=\Delta_0(fg)-\Delta_0(f)g-(-1)^{|f|}f\Delta_0(g),\qquad \Delta_0=-\partial_{K_0}\qquad [\text{C07, §10.1}],
with $\partial_\phi$ the order-two operator of [C07, §6.4]. It satisfies
the graded symmetry of [ESW, Def 1.15].
Remark 2.7.

The overall sign of $\langle\,,\rangle$ is a convention: reversing it reverses $K_0$ and the bracket, and leaves the master equation $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant. The relative signs of the three pairs are fixed by the master equation (Proposition [2.13](#b-00167)).
2.4 The action
Definition 2.8 (Action).
The action is the dimensional reduction of [ESW, (31)]:
S=\int_{\mathbb R^4}\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)+(d_Ac,A^*)+([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)+\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)\Big), \tag{2.1}
with
F_A=dA+\tfrac12[A\wedge A],\qquad d_A=d+[A,-],\qquad {\not d}_A=\rho\circ d_A .

Here $A$ is regarded as a one-form on $V_{10}$ constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$; $d$ acts along $\mathbb R^4$, and $d_A$, ${\not d}_A$ use all ten components of $A$. The pairing $(F_A,F_A)$ is the Hodge pairing on $\wedge^2V_{10}^\vee$ tensored with $(-,-)$ on $\mathfrak g$, normalised by

Every pairing in [(2.1)](#b-00108) is read with its left entry first, as printed in [ESW, (31)]. In [ESW] the full action is $S$ and the interaction is $I$; in [C07] the letter $S$ denotes the interaction. Here $S$ is always the full action and $I$ the interaction.
Splitting $A=A|_V+A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$,

(F_A,F_A)=(F_{A|_V},F_{A|_V})+\big(d_{A|_V}A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},\,d_{A|_V}A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\big)+\big(\tfrac12[A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\wedge A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}],\,\tfrac12[A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}\wedge A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}]\big),
{\not d}_A\lambda={\not d}\lambda+\rho([A|_V,\lambda])+\rho([A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},\lambda]),\qquad (d_Ac,A^*)=(dc,A^*|_V)+([A,c],A^*),
where $\rho([A,\lambda])$ is Clifford multiplication by the $V_{10}^\vee$ factor of $A$ (through the metric) together with $[-,-]$ on the $\mathfrak g$ factors, i.e. $({\not d}_A-{\not d})\lambda$.
Proposition 2.9 (Normalisation of the gauge kinetic term).
For $Q_1\in\Sigma$ put
S^{(1)}(Q_1)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)+\tfrac12(\rho(F_A)Q_1,\lambda^*)\Big)\qquad[\text{ESW, (33)}].

With the coefficient $-\tfrac14$ in front of the Hodge pairing $(F_A,F_A)$, the identity $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}=0$ of [ESW, Lemma 3.4] holds. With $+\tfrac14$, or with $-\tfrac12$ (the reading of $(F_A,F_A)$ as a sum over ordered pairs of directions, which doubles the Hodge pairing), it fails, already for abelian $\mathfrak g$ on the quadratic part of the action.
Proof.

Let $a$ be the coefficient of $(F_A,F_A)$. For abelian $\mathfrak g$ the bracket $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}$ is affine in $a$: the term $a(dA,dA)$ meets $-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair, $\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair, and $(dc,A^*)$ meets $\tfrac12(\rho(dA)Q_1,\lambda^*)$ in $(\rho(d\,dc)Q_1,\lambda^*)=0$. The explicit evaluation of this affine function, as a local functional modulo total derivatives, gives zero at $a=-\tfrac14$ and a nonzero functional at $a=+\tfrac14$ and at $a=-\tfrac12$; hence $a=-\tfrac14$ is its unique zero. For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$, $a=-\tfrac14$ and two sampled $Q_1\in\Sigma$ with small Gaussian-integer components, the density of $\{S,S^{(1)}(Q_1)\}$, a polynomial in the jets of all fields, has identically vanishing Euler–Lagrange derivatives, so the local functional vanishes. For general $\mathfrak g$ the identity is [ESW, Lemma 3.4] in ten dimensions, pulled back along the reduction [ESW, Prop 2.20]. ∎
The free part of $S$ is
\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle=\int\mathrm{dvol}\Big(-\tfrac14(dA,dA)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)+(dc,A^*)\Big), \tag{2.2}
and $I=S-\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$ is the interaction.
Remark 2.10 (Real slice).
The weight is $e^{+S/\hbar}$, with $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ negative definite on the real slice [C07, §6.6]. For $A$ real with respect to the compact real form of $\mathfrak g$,
\langle A,QA\rangle=-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)\le0,

and for fixed $p\neq0$ the quadratic form on the fibre $V_{10}^\vee$ has eigenvalues, in units of $(-,-)$, equal to $-\tfrac12|p|^2$ with multiplicity $9$ and $0$ with multiplicity $1$; the zero eigenvector is the longitudinal part of $A|_V$, which lies in $\operatorname{Im}Q$.

Fields are Fourier transformed as $\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}e^{i(p,x)}(\cdots)(p)$ and kernels on $\mathbb R^4\times\mathbb R^4$ as $\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}e^{i(p,x-y)}(\cdots)(p)$, with $p\in V$ and $|p|^2=(p,p)$; thus $d$ becomes $i(p,-)$.

2.7 The classical master equation
Proposition 2.13 (Classical master equation).
For every $\mathfrak g$ as in Definition [2.1](#b-00054):
• equivalently, $\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=0$ (that is, $Q^2=0$) and $QI+\tfrac12\{I,I\}=0$;

• if the sign of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pairing, or of the $(c^*,c)$ pairing, or of both, is reversed relative to the $(A,A^*)$ pairing in Definition [2.5](#b-00091), then $\{S,S\}\neq0$; reversing the sign of the term $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$ also gives $\{S,S\}\neq0$.
Proof.
Write $S=\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle+I$. Both summands are even, so by graded symmetry $\{I,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,I\}=QI$ (Proposition [2.11](#b-00133)), and
\{S,S\}=\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}+2\,QI+\{I,I\}.

The first term is $Q$ applied to $\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$; by the preservation of the pairing in Proposition [2.11](#b-00133), $\langle Qe,Qe\rangle=-(-1)^{|e|}\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$, so this term is a multiple of $\langle e,Q^2e\rangle$ and vanishes by $Q^2=0$. This gives the equivalence of the first two items.

Explicit evaluation. Take $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with an invariant pairing positive definite on the compact real form. The density of $\{S,S\}$, computed from Definitions [2.5](#b-00091)–[2.8](#b-00106) as a polynomial in the jets of all six fields with exact rational arithmetic, has identically vanishing Euler–Lagrange derivatives with respect to every field; hence $\{S,S\}=0$ as a local functional. The same holds separately for $\{\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle,\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle\}$ and for $2QI+\{I,I\}$, while $QI\neq0$. For each of the three other relative sign patterns of the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ and $(c^*,c)$ pairings, and for the reversed sign of $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$, the same computation gives a density with a nonvanishing Euler–Lagrange derivative.

General $\mathfrak g$. The action [(2.1)](#b-00108) is the BV action of the BRST theory of [ESW, Def 3.2], built as in [ESW, Def 1.34] with the natural pairing of the shifted cotangent bundle; it satisfies $\{S,S\}=0$ for every $\mathfrak g$, and the dimensional reduction preserves it [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56]. The natural pairing differs from Definition [2.5](#b-00091) at most by a sign on each of the three pairs, and these signs are independent of $\mathfrak g$. An overall sign leaves $\{S,S\}=0$ invariant, and by the explicit evaluation the pattern of Definition [2.5](#b-00091) is the unique one among the four relative patterns with $\{S,S\}=0$ for $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Hence the natural pairing coincides with Definition [2.5](#b-00091) up to an overall sign, and $\{S,S\}=0$ holds for every $\mathfrak g$. ∎
Remark 2.14 (Where the relative signs enter).
Decompose $\{S,S\}$ by the number of antifields. Each term is a product of a derivative along a field and a derivative along its partner, weighted by the sign of that pair.

• No antifield: the gauge variation of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\big(-\tfrac14(F_A,F_A)+\tfrac12(\lambda,{\not d}_A\lambda)\big)$ under $A\mapsto d_Ac$, $\lambda\mapsto[c,\lambda]$. The $A$-variation enters through the $(A,A^*)$ pair and the $\lambda$-variation through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair; gauge invariance cancels them for one relative sign of these two pairs.

• Linear in $A^*$: $[d_Ac,c]$ through the $(A,A^*)$ pair against $d_A(\tfrac12[c,c])$ through the $(c^*,c)$ pair; the Leibniz rule $d_A[c,c]=2[d_Ac,c]$ cancels them for one relative sign of these two pairs.

• Linear in $\lambda^*$: $[c,[c,\lambda]]$ through the $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ pair against $\tfrac12[[c,c],\lambda]$ through the $(c^*,c)$ pair; the Jacobi identity $2[c,[c,\lambda]]=[[c,c],\lambda]$ cancels them for the same relative signs.
• Linear in $c^*$: $[c,[c,c]]=0$.
3. Superconformal symmetry as an equivariant action

The dilatation of a composite operator, and every other superconformal transformation, acts on the fields of $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills theory up to gauge transformations and equations of motion. In the BV formalism this structure is a Maurer–Cartan element of a Chevalley–Eilenberg complex, an $L_\infty$ action in the sense of [ESW, Def 1.26–1.27], and it is the classical input of the equivariant observables used later. [ESW, (32)–(34), Thm 3.3] construct it for the Poincaré supersymmetry algebra; the special conformal transformations and the special supercharges require Weyl weights, a compensating term with the six scalars, and an R-symmetry rotation in the odd bracket. This chapter realises $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ on Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$, fixes the sign conventions of the complex, writes the action $S+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$, and states which components of its master equation hold for every gauge algebra and which were evaluated.
3.1 The algebra psl(4|4) in complexified Euclidean form

Throughout, $x\in V$ denotes the position on $\mathbb R^4$ and $E$ the Euler vector field $E(x)=x$ of [SW, (3)]; in this chapter $E$ always means this vector field. For a vector field $v$ on $V_{10}$, $(v,-)$ is its metric dual one-form, $L_v$ the Lie derivative, $v(-)$ the derivative along $v$, and $\operatorname{div}v$ the divergence, $L_v\,\mathrm{dvol}=(\operatorname{div}v)\,\mathrm{dvol}$.
Definition 3.1 (Even part).
The even part of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is the Lie algebra of vector fields on $V_{10}=V\oplus W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ spanned by
• translations $x\mapsto v_1$, $v_1\in V$;
• rotations $x\mapsto Xx$, $X\in\mathfrak{so}(V)$;
• the dilatation $\Delta=2E$;
• special conformal fields $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$, $v_1\in V$, the special conformal field of [SW, (3)] along $v_1$;
• linear vector fields on $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ given by elements of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$,
with the bracket $[v,v']=v(v')-v'(v)$. The first four kinds are the conformal Killing vector fields of $V$; together with $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ the even part has dimension $15+15=30$.
Definition 3.2 (Odd part).

The odd part of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is $\Pi(\Sigma\oplus\Sigma^*)$. An element $Q_1\in\Sigma$ is realised by the constant spinor $Q_1$, and an element $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ by the $\Sigma$-valued function $x\mapsto\rho(x)Q_2$. Together these span the conformal Killing spinors
x\mapsto Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\qquad Q_1\in\Sigma,\ Q_2\in\Sigma^* .
Supercharge spinors always carry a subscript, $Q_1,Q_2,\dots$, and each formula states whether they lie in $\Sigma$ or in $\Sigma^*$; the unsubscripted $Q$ is the differential of Chapter 1.
Definition 3.3 (Bracket).
The bracket of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ is:
• even with even: the bracket of vector fields, $[v,v']=v(v')-v'(v)$;
• even with odd:
[v,\,Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2]=v(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2)+\tfrac14\rho(d(v,-))(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2)-\tfrac18(\operatorname{div}v)(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2), \tag{3.1}
where $\rho$ of the two-form $d(v,-)$ means $\rho\circ q$ [ESW, (29)]; the right-hand side is again a conformal Killing spinor;
• odd with odd, for $Q_1,Q_3\in\Sigma$ and $Q_2,Q_4\in\Sigma^*$:
[Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\ Q_3+\rho(x)Q_4]=\Big(x\mapsto\Gamma\big(Q_1+\rho(x)Q_2,\,Q_3+\rho(x)Q_4\big)\big|_V\Big)+X, \tag{3.2}
where $|_V$ is the orthogonal projection $V_{10}\to V$ and $X\in\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ is defined by
(w,Xw')=(\rho(q(w\wedge w'))Q_1,Q_4)+(\rho(q(w\wedge w'))Q_3,Q_2),\qquad w,w'\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp .

The $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$-components of $\Gamma$ drop out of the bracket, as in the dimensional reduction of the supertranslation algebra [ESW, §2.6, Prop 2.20]; they reappear in $S^{(2)}$ (Definition [3.15](#b-00322)). The coefficient $1$ in front of the $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ component is the unique value for which the super-Jacobi identity holds on triples in $\Sigma\times\Sigma\times\Sigma^*$.
Proposition 3.4 (Brackets of the named generators).
• For $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, a translation; this is [ESW, Def 2.5] after reduction.
• For $Q_1,Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=-\big(x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$ with $v_1=\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)|_V$, a special conformal field.

• For $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $[Q_1,Q_2]=\big(x\mapsto\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)|_V\big)+X$ with $X$ as in Definition [3.3](#b-00200); the dilatation part of the first summand is $\tfrac12(Q_1,Q_2)\,\Delta$, and the rest is a rotation.
• For a translation $x\mapsto v_1$: $[v_1,Q_1]=0$ for $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and $[v_1,Q_2]=\rho(v_1)Q_2\in\Sigma$ for $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$.
• For a special conformal field $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$: its bracket with $Q_1\in\Sigma$ is $\rho(v_1)Q_1\in\Sigma^*$, and with $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ it is $0$.
• $[\Delta,Q_1]=-Q_1$ for $Q_1\in\Sigma$ and $[\Delta,Q_2]=+Q_2$ for $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$.
Proof.
The first two items follow from [(3.2)](#b-00207): for $Q_2=Q_4=0$ the $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ term vanishes; for $Q_1=Q_3=0$ it vanishes as well, and for $v\in V$
(v,\Gamma(\rho(x)Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2))=(\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)Q_1,Q_2)=2(v,x)(x,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2))-(x,x)(v,\Gamma(Q_1,Q_2)),
using $\rho(x)\rho(v)\rho(x)=2(v,x)\rho(x)-(x,x)\rho(v)$ from the Clifford relation and $(\rho(x)Q,Q')=(Q,\rho(x)Q')$. Projecting to $V$ gives $-\big((x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x\big)$.

For $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$ and $v\in V$, $(v,\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2))=(\rho(x)\rho(v)Q_1,Q_2)$; the part symmetric under $x\leftrightarrow v$ is $\tfrac12(\rho(x)\rho(v)+\rho(v)\rho(x))=(x,v)$, so the linear vector field $x\mapsto\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)|_V$ equals $(Q_1,Q_2)\,E=\tfrac12(Q_1,Q_2)\,\Delta$ plus an antisymmetric linear field, i.e. a rotation.

For the even–odd brackets use [(3.1)](#b-00204). Remark 3.6 (Dilatation normalisation).

The dilatation is the $\Delta$ of [SW, (17)], the vector field $2E$, with $\mathrm{ad}_\Delta$ eigenvalue $-2$ on translations, $+2$ on special conformal fields, $-1$ on $\Sigma$, $+1$ on $\Sigma^*$ and $0$ on rotations. The generator called $\Delta$ in [SW, (3)] is the vector field $-E$, and the bosonic part of the $\Delta$ of [SW, (12)] is $E$. Every cochain component is linear in its arguments, so a component evaluated on $2E$ is $-2$ times the same component evaluated on $-E$:
and a coefficient computed in the normalisation of [SW, (3)] is converted to the normalisation used here by the factor $-2$.
3.2 The Chevalley–Eilenberg complex and its sign conventions
Definition 3.7 (Cochains).
Following [ESW, Def 1.26] with the Lie algebra of loc. cit. taken to be $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$,
C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4),\mathcal O_{\rm loc}(\mathscr E))=\bigoplus_n\mathrm{Hom}(\wedge^n\mathfrak{psl}(4|4),\mathcal O_{\rm loc}(\mathscr E))[-n],
whose elements are multilinear maps $f$ of elements $x_1,x_2,\dots$ of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ (the notation of [ESW, Def 1.26]; the position $x$ carries no subscript) with the antisymmetry
[ESW, Def 1.26] prints the exponent $|x_1||x_2|+1$ [sic]. Here $|f|$ denotes the degree of $f$ in $C^\bullet$, and an element of degree $0$ has values $f(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ of parity $k+\sum_i|x_i|$.
Definition 3.8 (Cochain bracket and differential).
The cochain bracket is the formula of [ESW, Def 1.26]: $\{f,g\}(x_1,\dots,x_{k+l})$ is the sum over $(k,l)$-shuffles $\sigma$ of

\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\,\cdot\,(\text{Koszul sign of }\sigma)\,\cdot\,(-1)^{|g|k+\sum_{i=1}^k|x_{\sigma(i)}|(l+|g|)}\ \{f(x_{\sigma(1)},\dots,x_{\sigma(k)}),\,g(x_{\sigma(k+1)},\dots,x_{\sigma(k+l)})\},
with $\{-,-\}$ the bracket of Definition [2.6](#b-00095) and $|g|$ the degree of $g$ in $C^\bullet$. The Chevalley–Eilenberg differential is
(d_{CE}f)(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{|x_i|\sum_{p<i}|x_p|+|x_j|\sum_{p<j,\,p\neq i}|x_p|+i+j+|f|+1}\,f([x_i,x_j],x_1,\dots,\widehat{x_i},\dots,\widehat{x_j},\dots,x_n), \tag{3.3}
that is, the formula printed in [ESW, Def 1.26] multiplied by $-1$.

3.3 The Noether functionals
Definition 3.12 (Arity one).
For a conformal Killing vector field $v$ of $V$, or $v$ the linear vector field of an element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, regarded as a vector field on $V_{10}$:

Here $A$ is a one-form on $V_{10}$ constant along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ [ESW, Def 1.55, Prop 1.56] and $L_v$ is its Lie derivative on $V_{10}$: for $v$ on $V$, $L_v(A|_V)$ is the Lie derivative of the one-form and $L_v(\iota_wA)=v(\iota_wA)$; for $v$ given by $X\in\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$, $\iota_w(L_vA)=\iota_{Xw}A$.

where $\rho(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ is Clifford multiplication by the $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$-component of $A$, with its $\mathfrak g$ factor kept.

Example 3.13 (The dilatation).

For $\Delta=2E$: $(2E,-)=d(x,x)$ is closed, so $\rho(d(v,-))=0$, and $\operatorname{div}(2E)=8$. On the one-form $A|_V$, $L_{2E}A|_V=2E(A|_V)+2A|_V$ with $E(-)$ acting componentwise, and on the scalars $L_{2E}\iota_wA+\tfrac14\cdot8\,\iota_wA=2E(\iota_wA)+2\iota_wA$. Hence

in the normalisation of Remark [3.6](#b-00241), $A$, $\lambda$, $c$ carry the weights $2$, $3$, $0$, i.e. the Weyl weights $1$, $\tfrac32$, $0$ with respect to $E$.
Proposition 3.14 (The coefficients are forced).

Replace the coefficients $\tfrac14$ (spin), $\tfrac38$ (Weyl weight of $\lambda$) and $\tfrac14$ (Weyl weight of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$) in [(3.5)](#b-00299), and the coefficient $-1$ of the last term of [(3.7)](#b-00304), by unknowns. • a rotation in $\mathfrak{so}(V)$, and an element of $\mathfrak{so}(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$: spin coefficient $\tfrac14$;
• $\Delta$: $(\tfrac38,\tfrac14)$ for the two Weyl weights;
• a special conformal field: $(\tfrac14,\tfrac38,\tfrac14)$;

For each type the bracket $\{S,S^{(1)}(x_1)\}$ is affine in the unknowns. Its density, a polynomial in the jets of the fields with coefficients affine in the unknowns, was computed for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ at a sampled generator (drawn as in Proposition [3.18](#b-00341)); the conditions that all Euler–Lagrange derivatives vanish form a linear system whose unique solution is the one stated. • $Q_1\in\Sigma$, $Q_2\in\Sigma^*$: $\Gamma(Q_1,\rho(x)Q_2)$, linear in $x$;

Proposition 3.16 (The tower stops at arity two).
For every $\mathfrak g$ and every arguments, with $S^{(k\ge3)}=0$:
• the components of [(3.4)](#b-00273) of arity $\ge4$ hold;
• the arity-three components with at most one odd argument hold;
• the arity-three components with three odd arguments hold.
Proof.

$S^{(2)}$ contains the fields $A$, $\lambda^*$, $c^*$ and none of their partners $A^*$, $\lambda$, $c$, and the bracket pairs each field with its partner (Definition [2.6](#b-00095)); hence the first item. In arity $4$, with $S^{(3)}=S^{(4)}=0$, Lemma [3.11](#b-00275) leaves the three brackets $\{S^{(2)},S^{(2)}\}$, which vanish; when an argument is even, every surviving term contains $S^{(2)}$ with an even argument and vanishes. In arity $n\ge5$ every term contains $S^{(k)}$ with $k\ge3$ or $\{S^{(k)},S^{(l)}\}$ with $k+l=n$, hence $k\ge3$ or $l\ge3$, and vanishes. In arity $3$ with at most one odd argument, every term contains $S^{(2)}$ with an even entry, because among $[x_i,x_j]$ and $x_k$, and among any two of the arguments, at most one entry is odd; so every term vanishes. In arity $3$ with three odd arguments, every $[x_i,x_j]$ is even, so the equation of Lemma [3.11](#b-00275) reduces to the cyclic sum $\sum_{\rm cyc}\{S^{(1)}(x_1),S^{(2)}(x_2,x_3)\}$. In this bracket, $S^{(2)}$ supplies $A$ and $\lambda^*$, whose partners $A^*$ and $\lambda$ occur in $S^{(1)}(x_1)$ exclusively through the term $-(\Gamma(Q_1,\lambda),A^*)$, with $Q_1$ replaced by the conformal Killing spinor of $x_1$; the last term of [(3.7)](#b-00304) contains $A$ and $\lambda^*$ and has vanishing bracket with $S^{(2)}$. Remark 3.19 (Random-draw bound).

Each component of [(3.4)](#b-00273) is multilinear in its arguments. If such a multilinear defect is nonzero, its value at independent uniform draws vanishes with probability at most $\sum_j1/|S_j|$, where $S_j$ is the set from which the coordinates of the $j$-th argument are drawn (the Schwartz–Zippel bound, applied one argument at a time); an argument of type $\Delta$ contributes $0$, because a nonzero linear function of a nonzero multiple of $\Delta$ is nonzero. With $|S_j|=4$ for even and $15$ for odd arguments, the bound per sampled point is

\tfrac14\ (\text{one even}),\qquad \tfrac1{15}\ (\text{one odd}),\qquad \tfrac12,\ \tfrac{19}{60},\ \tfrac2{15}\ (\text{even--even, even--odd, odd--odd}),\qquad \tfrac{23}{60}\ (\text{even, odd, odd}).
The arity-three components with three odd arguments and all components of arity $\ge4$ hold for every argument by Proposition [3.16](#b-00330).

4. Costello's data with a UV boundary only

Costello's renormalisation needs a gauge-fixing operator $Q^{GF}$, the heat kernel of $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$ and the propagator $P(\varepsilon,T)$, and its axioms [C07, Def 4.3.3] are formulated on a compact manifold; [C07, §5.2] records that Yang–Mills theory in second-order form lies outside them. On Euclidean $\mathbb R^4$ we keep a single regulator, the lower Schwinger limit $\varepsilon$, set the upper limit to $\infty$, and introduce no infrared scale. This chapter constructs a Feynman-gauge operator $Q^{GF}$ that satisfies three of the five axioms, identifies the two that fail, and proves the identities that hold with these data: $QP(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon$, the UV-boundary identity, the acyclicity of $Q$ at scale $\infty$, and the one-loop formula for the graph expansion.

Proposition 4.2 (The Laplacian).
• $H:=[Q,Q^{GF}]=QQ^{GF}+Q^{GF}Q=d^*d\otimes\mathrm{id}$ on every component of every slot, $d^*d$ being the positive Laplacian on functions on $\mathbb R^4$; in momentum space $H=|p|^2$.

\begin{aligned}

A:&\quad QQ^{GF}A=Q\big(-d^*(A|_V)\big)=dd^*(A|_V),\qquad Q^{GF}QA=Q^{GF}\big(-\tfrac12d^*dA\big)=d^*dA;\\
A^*:&\quad QQ^{GF}A^*=Q(-2A^*)=d^*dA^*,\qquad Q^{GF}QA^*=Q^{GF}\big(d^*(A^*|_V)\big)=dd^*(A^*|_V);\\

For all $e_0,e_1\in\mathscr E_c$,
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle,\qquad \langle Qe_0,e_1\rangle=-(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Qe_1\rangle ;

equivalently $(Q^{GF}\otimes1-1\otimes Q^{GF})K_0=0$ and $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_0=0$. Thus $Q^{GF}$ has the adjointness opposite to that of $Q$, which is the relation between "self adjoint" $Q$ [C07, §4.3] and "skew self adjoint" $Q^{GF}$ [C07, Def 4.3.3(1)].

The statement for $Q$ is Proposition [2.11](#b-00133). For $Q^{GF}$ the pairing vanishes outside the following cases. For $e_0,e_1$ in the $A^*$ slot (odd),
\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1),\qquad \langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle=-\langle-2e_1,e_0\rangle=2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,e_1).

For $e_0,e_1$ in the $\lambda^*$ slot (even), with the symmetry of $\rho(v)$ and integration by parts,
The case $e_0$ in the $c^*$ slot, $e_1$ in the $A$ slot follows by graded antisymmetry. In each case $\langle Q^{GF}e_0,e_1\rangle=(-1)^{|e_0|}\langle e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle$. ∎
Proposition 4.4 (Status of the gauge-fixing axioms).
Of the conditions of [C07, Def 4.3.3]:
• (1) holds: Proposition [4.3](#b-00378);
• (2) holds: every component of $Q^{GF}$ has order $0$ or $1$;
• (3) fails: $(Q^{GF})^2$ vanishes on the slots of $c$, $A$, $\lambda$, $\lambda^*$, and
(Q^{GF})^2A^*=2\,d^*(A^*|_V)\ \ (\text{in the slot of }c),\qquad (Q^{GF})^2c^*=-2\,dc^*\ \ (\text{in the slot of }A|_V);
• (4) holds: $H=d^*d\otimes\mathrm{id}$ is a generalised Laplacian (Proposition [4.2](#b-00370));
• (5) fails: $\operatorname{Im}Q\cap\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}\neq0$, since for every nonzero $c\in\mathscr E_c$ in the ghost slot
Qc=-dc=Q^{GF}\big(\tfrac12dc\ \text{in the slot of }A^*|_V\big).

Moreover $\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}$ fails to be isotropic for $\langle\,,\rangle$: for $e_0$ in the $A^*$ slot and $e_1$ in the $c^*$ slot, $\langle Q^{GF}e_0,Q^{GF}e_1\rangle=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(e_0,de_1)$.
Proof.

$(Q^{GF})^2A^*=Q^{GF}(-2A^*)=-2\big(-d^*(A^*|_V)\big)$ and $(Q^{GF})^2c^*=Q^{GF}(dc^*)=-2\,dc^*$; on the other slots the image of $Q^{GF}$ lies in the slots of $c$ and $\lambda$, where $Q^{GF}$ vanishes. For (5), $Q^{GF}(\tfrac12dc)=-2\cdot\tfrac12dc$. The last formula is $\langle-2e_0,de_1\rangle$ with $-2e_0$ in the $A$ slot. ∎
Remark 4.5 (Consequences of the two failures).

Three statements of [C07] use (3) or (5) and are unavailable here: [C07, Lemma 6.5.1] ($P(0,\infty)$ inverts $Q\colon\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}\to\operatorname{Im}Q$; its proof uses $(Q^{GF})^2=0$), the real-slice Gaussian over $(\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF})_{\mathbb R}$ of [C07, §6.6], and [C07, Lemma 6.6.2]. Indeed $\operatorname{Im}Q^{GF}$ contains the whole $A$ slot, on which $\langle e,Qe\rangle$ has the longitudinal zero eigenvector (Chapter 1). Every statement below uses $Q^2=0$, $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$, $[Q,H]=0$ and the adjointness relations, and none of (3), (5). The homotopy identity of Theorem [4.16](#b-00469) is what survives of [C07, Lemma 6.5.1].
Remark 4.6 (Feynman gauge).

In momentum space the $A\otimes A$ component of the propagator $P(0,\infty)$ (Proposition [4.10](#b-00422) at $\varepsilon=0$) is $2(-,-)^{-1}\otimes(\text{inverse metric of }V_{10})\,|p|^{-2}$. It is the inverse of the second variation of $-\big(\tfrac12\langle A,QA\rangle-\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)\big)=\tfrac14\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,HA)$, i.e. the covariance of the weight $e^{+S/\hbar}$ for the Yang–Mills kinetic term completed by the Feynman-gauge term $-\tfrac14(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$; it has the eigenvalue $2(-,-)^{-1}|p|^{-2}$, positive, in all ten directions of $V_{10}$. Restricted to $\lambda$, the propagator $P(0,\infty)$ is minus the inverse of the second variation of $\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$.
4.2 Heat kernel and propagator
Definition 4.7 (Heat kernel).

For $t>0$, $K_t\in\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ is the kernel with the components of $K_0$ (Definition [2.6](#b-00095)) with $\delta(x-y)$ replaced by $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$; in momentum space this factor is $e^{-t|p|^2}$. Then $K_t\star e=e^{-tH}e$ [C07, §6.5; C07, §15.2]. The kernel
L_t=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t
represents $Q^{GF}e^{-tH}$ [C07, §6.5]. On $\mathbb R^4$,
K_\infty:=\lim_{t\to\infty}K_t=0,
pointwise in $x-y$, and in momentum space for every $p\neq0$.
Proposition 4.8 (Heat-kernel identities).
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_t=0,\qquad \frac{d}{dt}K_t+(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t=0\qquad[\text{C07, §6.5}].
Proof.

$K_t=(e^{-tH}\otimes1)K_0$, $[Q,H]=0$ and $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)K_0=0$ give the first identity. For the second, odd operators on different tensor factors anticommute, $(1\otimes Q)(Q^{GF}\otimes1)=-(Q^{GF}\otimes1)(1\otimes Q)$, and $(1\otimes Q)K_t=-(Q\otimes1)K_t$, so
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t=(QQ^{GF}\otimes1)K_t+(Q^{GF}Q\otimes1)K_t=(H\otimes1)K_t=-\frac{d}{dt}K_t .
Definition 4.9 (Propagator).
P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty L_t\,dt=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t\,dt\qquad[\text{C07, §6.5}],\qquad \varepsilon>0 .

The component in the row $X\otimes Y$ below is the value of $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ [C07, §6.4] on the product of a coordinate functional of $X$ at $x$ and one of $Y$ at $y$, in this order.
Proposition 4.10 (Components of the propagator).
The scalar factor of $K_t$ integrates to
\int_\varepsilon^\infty(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}\,dt=\frac{1-e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}}{4\pi^2|x-y|^2},\qquad \int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t|p|^2}\,dt=\frac{e^{-\varepsilon|p|^2}}{|p|^2},
and the nonzero components of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ are:

Proof.
With $u=|x-y|^2/4t$, $dt=-\frac{|x-y|^2}{4u^2}du$, and
\int_\varepsilon^\infty\frac{e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}}{16\pi^2t^2}\,dt=\frac{1}{4\pi^2|x-y|^2}\int_0^{|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}e^{-u}\,du=\frac{1-e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}}{4\pi^2|x-y|^2}.

The components follow from $L_t=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_t$ and Definition [4.1](#b-00366), with $Q^{GF}$ acting on the first factor at $x$ and no Koszul sign. The $A^*\otimes A$ component of $K_t$, $-(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$ times the identity, is sent by $A^*\mapsto-2A^*$ to $+2(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4t}$ in $A\otimes A$. The $A|_V\otimes A^*|_V$ component is sent by $A\mapsto-d^*(A|_V)$, the divergence of $A|_V$ in the first factor, to $-d_x$ of the scalar factor in $c\otimes A^*|_V$. The $c^*\otimes c$ component is sent by $c^*\mapsto dc^*$ to $-d_x$ of the scalar factor in $A^*|_V\otimes c$. Graded symmetry: for $c\otimes A^*|_V$ and $A^*|_V\otimes c$ the Koszul sign is $-1$ and the gradient of the even scalar factor is odd under $x\leftrightarrow y$; for $\lambda\otimes\lambda$ the Koszul sign is $-1$ and $\rho(-p)=-\rho(p)$. ∎
Proposition 4.11 (The two UV-boundary kernels).
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=K_\varepsilon, \tag{4.1}
\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon . \tag{4.2}
Proof.
By Proposition [4.8](#b-00413),
(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)L_t\,dt=-\int_\varepsilon^\infty\frac{d}{dt}K_t\,dt=K_\varepsilon-K_\infty=K_\varepsilon .

This is [C07, Lemma 10.2.1] with the upper scale at $\infty$ and $K_\infty=0$. In position space the scalar core of [(4.1)](#b-00436) is $d^*d\,\frac{1-e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}}{4\pi^2|x-y|^2}=(4\pi\varepsilon)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4\varepsilon}$. The second identity is the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to $\int_\varepsilon^\infty L_t\,dt$. ∎
Remark 4.12 (Two objects at $t=\varepsilon$).

The lower end of the Schwinger integral carries two different kernels. By [(4.2)](#b-00437), $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$ governs the $\varepsilon$-dependence of every graph: for a graph value $\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E}}f$ over its edges, $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ is minus the sum over edges of $\varepsilon f$ with that edge pinned at $t=\varepsilon$, i.e. carrying $L_\varepsilon$. The singular coefficients ($\varepsilon^{-1}$, $\log\varepsilon$) and the scaling behaviour therefore sit on $L_\varepsilon$ edges. By [(4.1)](#b-00436), $K_\varepsilon$ governs the action of $Q$ (Theorem [4.14](#b-00448)): the obstruction to the quantum master equation and the $Q$-variation of observables sit on $K_\varepsilon$ edges.
4.3 The UV-boundary identity
Definition 4.13 (Scale-$\varepsilon$ Laplacian and bracket).

\Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}\quad[\text{C07, §10.1}],\qquad \{f,g\}_\varepsilon=\Delta_\varepsilon(fg)-\Delta_\varepsilon(f)g-(-1)^{|f|}f\Delta_\varepsilon(g)\quad[\text{CG2, §7.2.8}],
the second with the Laplacian $\Delta_\varepsilon$ of [C07] in the product rule of [CG2]. Since $K_\infty=0$, $\Delta_\infty=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$.
Theorem 4.14 (UV-boundary identity).
On functionals with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))$ (Chapter 2), as formal power series in $\hbar$,
(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\,(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon). \tag{4.3}
This holds with the operator $Q^{GF}$ of Definition [4.1](#b-00366), for which $(Q^{GF})^2\neq0$.
Proof.
By [C07, §6.4], $[\partial_\phi,Q]=\partial_{Q\phi}$ for $\phi\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$, with $Q$ acting on $\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ as $Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q$. With [(4.1)](#b-00436),

\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}Q-Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{K_\varepsilon}=-\Delta_\varepsilon ,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}Q+\Delta_\varepsilon .
The operators $\partial_\phi$ mutually commute [C07, §6.4], so $\Delta_\varepsilon$ commutes with $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$, and by induction on $n$
Q\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^n=\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^nQ+n\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}^{n-1}\Delta_\varepsilon .
Multiplying by $\hbar^n/n!$ and summing over $n$,
Q\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}Q+\hbar\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\Delta_\varepsilon .

Finally $d_{CE}$ acts on the arguments in $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ and $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ on the fields; $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ contains no superconformal ghost, so $[\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)},d_{CE}]=0$. Each step uses $Q^2=0$, [(4.1)](#b-00436) and the algebra of the operators $\partial_\phi$; none uses $(Q^{GF})^2$. ∎
Corollary 4.15 (Master equations at the two ends).

Let $J$ be an even functional with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))[[\hbar]]$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$ when the arguments of the cochains are counted as fields, as in [CG2, §13.2.2], and $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}\big)$ (Definition [4.19](#b-00491)). Then
(d_{CE}+Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon)e^{J/\hbar}=0\iff(d_{CE}+Q)\,e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}=0,
and the two sides are equivalent to
(d_{CE}+Q)J+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J=0,\qquad (d_{CE}+Q)\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=0 .
Proof.

Apply [(4.3)](#b-00450) to $e^{J/\hbar}$; the operator $e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}$ is invertible. This is [C07, Lemma 10.2.2] with the second scale at $\infty$, where $\Delta_\infty=0$. For an even $J$, the product rule of Definition [4.13](#b-00445), applied to the powers $J^n$, gives $\Delta_\varepsilon e^{J/\hbar}=e^{J/\hbar}\big(\hbar^{-1}\Delta_\varepsilon J+\tfrac12\hbar^{-2}\{J,J\}_\varepsilon\big)$, while $d_{CE}+Q$ is a derivation, $(d_{CE}+Q)e^{J/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}e^{J/\hbar}(d_{CE}+Q)J$; this is the equivalence of [C07, §10.1] with $\Delta_\varepsilon$ in place of $\Delta_0$. ∎
4.4 Acyclicity at scale infinity

For a kernel $\phi\in\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ write $\phi\star$ for the operator it represents [C07, §6.3]. Thus $K_t\star=e^{-tH}$, and $P(\varepsilon,\infty)\star=\int_\varepsilon^\infty Q^{GF}e^{-tH}dt$; $P(0,\infty)\star$ is the limit $\varepsilon\to0$.
Theorem 4.16 (Acyclicity of $Q$ at scale $\infty$).
For every $\alpha\in\mathscr E_c$ the integral $P(0,\infty)\star\alpha=\int_0^\infty Q^{GF}e^{-tH}\alpha\,dt$ converges to a smooth section, and
Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha\big)+P(0,\infty)\star(Q\alpha)=\alpha . \tag{4.4}
In kernel form, $(Q\otimes1+1\otimes Q)P(0,\infty)=K_0$. In particular every $\alpha\in\mathscr E_c$ with $Q\alpha=0$ is $Q$-exact: $\alpha=Q\big(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha\big)$.
Proof.

Each component of $e^{-tH}\alpha$ is the convolution of a component of $\alpha$ with $(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x|^2/4t}$, so $e^{-tH}\alpha$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $(4\pi t)^{-2}$ times $L^1$ norms of $\alpha$ and its first derivatives, and by the supremum norms of the same for $t\le1$. Since $Q^{GF}$ has constant coefficients and order at most $1$, $\|Q^{GF}e^{-tH}\alpha\|_\infty$ is integrable on $(0,\infty)$; the same bounds for the derivatives allow $Q$ to pass under the integral. Since $[Q,H]=0$, $Q^{GF}e^{-tH}Q\alpha=Q^{GF}Qe^{-tH}\alpha$, and
The limit vanishes because $|e^{-TH}\alpha|\le(4\pi T)^{-2}\|\alpha\|_{L^1}$; this is $K_\infty=0$. The kernel form is [(4.1)](#b-00436) at $\varepsilon\to0$ with $K_\varepsilon\to K_0$. ∎
For the consequence on functionals, let $Q_{(n)}=\sum_{i=1}^n1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes Q\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)}$ be the tensor-product differential on $\mathscr E^{\otimes n}$ [C07, §6.2], and
h_{(n)}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n1^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes P(0,\infty)\star\otimes1^{\otimes(n-i)},

with the Koszul rule for odd operators on tensor factors. For an $n$-linear graded-symmetric functional $F$ of parity $|F|$, the derivation $Q$ of [C07, §6.2] acts by $QF=(-1)^{|F|}F\circ Q_{(n)}$: in $F(e+\epsilon Qe,\dots)$ with $e$ even and $\epsilon$ odd, the parameter $\epsilon$ passes through $F$.
Corollary 4.17 (Functionals at scale $\infty$).

Let $n\ge1$ and let $F$ be a graded-symmetric $n$-linear functional on $\big(\mathscr E_c+P(0,\infty)\star\mathscr E_c\big)^{\otimes n}$ with $F\circ Q_{(n)}=0$ there. Then on $\mathscr E_c^{\otimes n}$
F=(F\circ h_{(n)})\circ Q_{(n)}=(-1)^{|F|+1}\,Q\big(F\circ h_{(n)}\big).
Hence the complex of functionals of this type modulo constants is acyclic for $Q$: every $Q$-closed functional without constant term is $Q$-exact.
Proof.

The space $\mathscr E_c+P(0,\infty)\star\mathscr E_c$ is stable under $Q$, since $Q(P(0,\infty)\star\alpha)=\alpha-P(0,\infty)\star Q\alpha$. On $\mathscr E_c^{\otimes n}$, odd operators acting on different tensor factors anticommute, so the graded commutator of the $j$-th copy of $Q$ with the $i$-th copy of $P(0,\infty)\star$ vanishes for $i\neq j$, and for $i=j$ it is the identity of the $i$-th factor by [(4.4)](#b-00471). Hence
Q_{(n)}h_{(n)}+h_{(n)}Q_{(n)}=\frac1n\sum_{i,j}\big(Q_jh_i+h_iQ_j\big)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{id}=\mathrm{id}

on $\mathscr E_c^{\otimes n}$, where $Q_j$, $h_i$ denote the operators on the $j$-th, $i$-th factor. Composing with $F$ and using $F\circ Q_{(n)}=0$ on the extended space gives $F=(F\circ h_{(n)})\circ Q_{(n)}$, and $F\circ h_{(n)}$ has parity $|F|+1$, so $(F\circ h_{(n)})\circ Q_{(n)}=(-1)^{|F|+1}Q(F\circ h_{(n)})$. ∎
Remark 4.18 (Where the content of an operator lies).

At scale $\infty$ the differential on functionals is $d_{CE}+Q$ ($\Delta_\infty=0$, $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$), and Corollary [4.17](#b-00480) shows that $Q$ alone has trivial cohomology on functionals without constant term: every $Q$-closed functional at scale $\infty$ is $Q$-exact, so an arbitrary functional $O(\varepsilon)$ produces a class that carries no information. The content of an operator is the local functional $O(\varepsilon)$ at the UV end whose flow to scale $\infty$ has an $\varepsilon\to0$ limit. This requirement fixes the singular part of $O(\varepsilon)$ uniquely; the finite part is the scheme freedom. Correspondingly, an equation $Q\,O[\infty]=Y[\infty]$ between observables at scale $\infty$ has content because $Y$ is required to be local, and anomalous dimensions are classes in the cohomology of local functionals.
4.5 The graph expansion and the one-loop formula
Definition 4.19 (Renormalisation group flow).
For an even $\phi\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$ and an even functional $J$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$,
W(\phi,J)=\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_\phi}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\qquad[\text{CG2, §7.2.7}],

which is $\Gamma(\phi,J)$ of [C07, Def 6.6.1]. The letter $W$ with two arguments always denotes this flow; $W$ alone is the multiplicity space of [ESW, §10], and $\Gamma$ is reserved for the $\Gamma$-pairing of [ESW, (28)].
Proposition 4.20 (Graph expansion).
For $J=\sum_{i\ge0}\hbar^iJ_i$ as in Definition [4.19](#b-00491),
W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\sum_\gamma\hbar^{\,b_1(\gamma)+\sum_v\deg v}\,\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,w_\gamma\qquad[\text{C07, §15.4}],

the sum over connected graphs $\gamma$ with legs, each vertex $v$ labelled by a Taylor component of $J_{\deg v}$ (vertices of degree $0$ at least trivalent), each edge by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, each leg by an argument; $|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$ counts the automorphisms fixing the legs, and $w_\gamma$ is obtained from the full multilinear vertex functions, contracted along the edges and summed over all component labels. Edge rule: two contracted coordinate functionals, brought adjacent by Koszul reordering, are replaced by the component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ in the same order (Definition [4.9](#b-00419)). At order $\hbar^1$ either $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and all vertices have degree $0$, or $b_1(\gamma)=0$ and exactly one vertex has degree $1$, for instance a counterterm vertex.
Proof.

Expanding the exponentials, a term of $e^{\hbar\partial_{P}}e^{J/\hbar}$ is a set of vertices, each a factor $\hbar^{\deg v-1}J_{\deg v}$, with $E$ pairs of half-edges contracted by $\hbar\partial_P$; the factor $\frac12$ in $\partial_P=\frac12\sum\partial_{P''}\partial_{P'}$ [C07, §6.4] and the factorials of the exponentials combine to $1/|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|$, and on two coordinate functionals $\partial_P$ returns the component of $P$ in their order. The logarithm keeps the connected graphs, and the overall factor $\hbar$ gives the power $\hbar^{1+E-V+\sum_v\deg v}=\hbar^{b_1+\sum_v\deg v}$ with $b_1=E-V+1$. The last statement is $b_1+\sum_v\deg v=1$. ∎

For the one-loop formula let $\mathscr E$ be a finite-dimensional super vector space, as for $M$ a point in [C07, §6.6, §10.1], with $P=\sum P'\otimes P''\in\mathrm{Sym}^2\mathscr E$ even and $J$ an even quadratic functional on $\mathscr E$. Define the linear map $M\colon\mathscr E\to\mathscr E$ by
M(e)=\sum P'\,(-1)^{|P''|}\,\partial_{P''}\partial_eJ ,

i.e. $P$ composed with the parity operator $(-1)^{|\cdot|}$ composed with the second derivative of $J$, the right-hand slot differentiated first. $\mathrm{STr}$ is the supertrace on $\mathrm{End}(\mathscr E)$ [CG2, §13.7.2].
Proposition 4.21 (One-loop formula).
If the coefficients of $J$ are complex numbers, then, as formal power series in $J$,
\hbar\log\big(e^{\hbar\partial_P}e^{J/\hbar}\big)\Big|_{0}=-\frac\hbar2\,\mathrm{STr}\log(1-M)=\hbar\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{2n}\,\mathrm{STr}(M^n). \tag{4.5}
The term $n=1$ is $\hbar\,\partial_PJ$, and the term of order $n$ is the sum of the cycles with $n$ vertices.
Proof.

At the origin the surviving terms are those with as many contractions as vertices, so the left side is $\hbar\log\sum_m(m!)^{-2}\partial_P^mJ^m$, independent of $\hbar$ inside the logarithm. For $n=1$: $\tfrac12\mathrm{STr}(M)=\tfrac12\sum P'\,(-1)^{|P''|+|P'|}\,\partial_{P''}\partial_{P'}J=\partial_PJ$, because $P$ is even and $\partial_P=\frac12\sum\partial_{P''}\partial_{P'}$ [C07, §6.4].

Both sides of [(4.5)](#b-00506) are, order by order in $J$, polynomials in the coefficients of $P$ and $J$, so it suffices to prove the identity on a Zariski-dense set. An even quadratic $J$ with complex coefficients and an even $P$ have no mixed even–odd part: $\mathscr E=\mathscr E^{\rm ev}\oplus\mathscr E^{\rm odd}$, $J=J^{\rm ev}+J^{\rm odd}$, $P=P^{\rm ev}+P^{\rm odd}$, the operators $\partial_{P^{\rm ev}}$, $\partial_{P^{\rm odd}}$ commute, and both sides factorise, with $M=M^{\rm ev}\oplus M^{\rm odd}$ and $\mathrm{STr}=\mathrm{tr}_{\rm ev}-\mathrm{tr}_{\rm odd}$. For generic data the even block has a basis diagonalising both the symmetric form $(P^{\rm ev})^{-1}$ and the second derivative of $J^{\rm ev}$ (the eigenvectors of $M^{\rm ev}$ for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal for $(P^{\rm ev})^{-1}$), and the odd block splits into two-dimensional subspaces orthogonal for both antisymmetric forms (the eigenspaces of $M^{\rm odd}$, each of dimension $2$ generically, are orthogonal for $(P^{\rm odd})^{-1}$ since $M^{\rm odd}$ is self-adjoint for it). Both sides are additive over such orthogonal splittings, so two cases remain.
One even direction $e$, with coordinate $\varphi$ and complex numbers $a,b$, $P=a\,e\otimes e$, $J=\tfrac12b\,\varphi^2$: $\partial_P=\tfrac a2\partial^2$, $M=ab$, and
\sum_m\frac{\partial_P^mJ^m}{(m!)^2}=\sum_m\frac{(a/2)^m(b/2)^m(2m)!}{(m!)^2}=\sum_m\binom{2m}{m}\Big(\frac{ab}4\Big)^m=(1-ab)^{-1/2},
so the left side is $-\frac\hbar2\log(1-ab)=-\frac\hbar2\mathrm{STr}\log(1-M)$.

Two odd directions $e_1,e_2$, with coordinates $\vartheta_1,\vartheta_2$ and complex numbers $a,b$, $P=a(e_1\otimes e_2-e_2\otimes e_1)$, $J=b\,\vartheta_1\vartheta_2$: here $\partial_P=a\,\partial_{e_2}\partial_{e_1}$, $J^2=0$, and $\partial_PJ=ab$, so the left side is $\hbar\log(1+ab)$. The second derivatives are $\partial_{e_2}\partial_{e_1}J=b$, $\partial_{e_1}\partial_{e_2}J=-b$, $\partial_{e_i}\partial_{e_i}J=0$, hence

M(e_1)=-\big(a\,e_1\,\partial_{e_2}\partial_{e_1}J-a\,e_2\,\partial_{e_1}\partial_{e_1}J\big)=-ab\,e_1,\qquad M(e_2)=-\big(a\,e_1\,\partial_{e_2}\partial_{e_2}J-a\,e_2\,\partial_{e_1}\partial_{e_2}J\big)=-ab\,e_2,
and $-\frac\hbar2\mathrm{STr}\log(1-M)=+\frac\hbar2\cdot2\log(1+ab)=\hbar\log(1+ab)$. ∎
Remark 4.22 (Use in the field theory; odd backgrounds).

For the one-loop part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I)$ at a background field configuration, $J$ is the part of $I(\text{background}+\text{fluctuation})$ quadratic in the fluctuation, $P=P(\varepsilon,\infty)$, $\mathrm{STr}$ includes the trace over $\mathfrak g$ and the integration over positions, and expanding in the background produces the one-loop one-particle-irreducible graphs with their external legs; the parity operator and the supertrace produce the signs of fermion and ghost loops. When the background contains odd fields, the coefficients of $J$ lie in an auxiliary supercommutative algebra with odd elements. Formula [(4.5)](#b-00506) in that setting was checked by exact expansion to third order in $J$ on super vector spaces of dimensions $(2|2)$ and $(1|2)$ with even and odd backgrounds; there the variant without the parity operator and the variant with the trace in place of the supertrace both fail.
5. Counterterms at one loop and the QME at the UV boundary

The counterterm of [C07, Thm B] is unique: its singular part is fixed by the requirement that the flow $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ have a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$. The regulator, however, cuts every edge at the Schwinger time $\varepsilon$ and breaks the gauge symmetry, so the one-loop counterterm contains the mass terms $\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$, whose $Q$-variation is nonzero. Transported to the UV boundary by Theorem [4.14](#b-00448), the quantum master equation then fails by a finite local functional, and a finite local counterterm has to be chosen to remove it: this is the first renormalisation condition of the theory. This chapter computes $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in every one-loop sector of superficial degree $\ge0$, identifies its $\log\varepsilon$ part as a rescaling of the fields with vanishing component along the coupling, and evaluates the master equation at the UV boundary in the sector with legs $(c,A|_V)$, where the first finite counterterm appears.
5.1 The one-loop counterterm and its boundary form

Throughout this chapter $\mathfrak g$ is simple. Then the Killing form $\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)$ is a multiple of the invariant pairing, and the ratio $\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$, for $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,Y)\neq0$, is a number independent of $X$ and $Y$. Every one-loop coefficient of this chapter is a rational multiple of
\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)},

except the coefficients of the fourth-order adjoint traces of the quartic graphs, which are rational multiples of $\hbar/16\pi^2$. External momenta are generic and nonzero, and the upper Schwinger limit is $\infty$ (Chapter 3).
Definition 5.1 (One-loop counterterm).

For a connected graph $\gamma$ with legs, $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and all vertices labelled by $I$ (Proposition [4.20](#b-00495)), let $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ be its value with every edge labelled by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §15.4]. When, as $\varepsilon\to0$, $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ is the sum of a multiple of $\varepsilon^{-1}$, a multiple of $\log\varepsilon$, and a functional with a limit, $\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ denotes the sum of the first two terms [CG2, §13.7.2]. The one-loop counterterm is
I^{CT}[\varepsilon]=\hbar\sum_\gamma\frac{1}{|\operatorname{Aut}\gamma|}\,\mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon\,w_\gamma(\varepsilon), \tag{5.1}

the sum over the one-particle-irreducible graphs $\gamma$ with $b_1(\gamma)=1$ and at least two legs, modulo constants. Its coefficients lie in the span of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$, the one-loop part of the renormalisation scheme $\mathscr A_{<0}$ [C07, Def 1.4.1; CG2, §13.7.2].
Remark 5.2 (Relation with Theorem B).

[C07, Thm B] constructs the counterterm on a compact manifold with a finite upper scale, order by order in the number of legs: at one loop, its part with $k$ legs is the singular part of the order-$\hbar$, $k$-leg part of the flow of the interaction minus the counterterms with fewer legs. Here the interaction $I$ of [(2.3)](#b-00153) is even, local and at least cubic, the upper scale is $\infty$, and the singular parts are computed graph by graph; locality is a computed property, established below in every sector. A one-particle-reducible one-loop graph is a one-particle-irreducible one-loop subgraph with trees attached along edges $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$. Grouped with the same trees attached to the counterterm vertex of the subgraph, it has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$; a subgraph with one leg carries the colour factor $\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X)=0$. Hence [(5.1)](#b-00527) is the one-loop counterterm of [C07, Thm B], and the order-$\hbar$ part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$.

The $\varepsilon$-dependence of a graph is carried by the lower ends of its Schwinger integrals. By [(4.2)](#b-00437), $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-L_\varepsilon$ with $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$.
Proposition 5.3 (Boundary form of the scale derivative).
Let $\gamma$ be a graph with edge set $E(\gamma)$ [C07, §15.5], and let $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)$ be its value with every edge labelled by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$. Then

\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\sum_{e\in E(\gamma)}w_\gamma\big(\text{edge }e\text{ labelled by }-\varepsilon L_\varepsilon,\ \text{the other edges by }P(\varepsilon,\infty)\big). \tag{5.2}

In the Schwinger form $w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)}}f_\gamma\prod_{e}dt_e$ of [C07, §15.5], with the edge $e$ carrying $L_{t_e}$, the $e$-th term of [(5.2)](#b-00534) is
-\varepsilon\int_{[\varepsilon,\infty)^{E(\gamma)\setminus\{e\}}}f_\gamma\big|_{t_e=\varepsilon}\prod_{e'\neq e}dt_{e'} .
Proof.
The value $w_\gamma$ is multilinear in the kernels labelling the edges, so the Leibniz rule gives
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma=\sum_e w_\gamma\Big(\text{edge }e\text{ labelled by }\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)\Big),

and $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-L_\varepsilon$ by [(4.2)](#b-00437). In the Schwinger form, $\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int_\varepsilon^\infty(\cdots)\,dt_e=-(\cdots)|_{t_e=\varepsilon}$ for each edge. ∎
Corollary 5.4 (Singular part from the boundary).
If the right-hand side of [(5.2)](#b-00534) equals $-a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b+O(\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon$-independent functionals $a$, $b$, then

w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b\log\varepsilon+(\text{a functional with a limit})+O(\varepsilon),\qquad \mathrm{Sing}_\varepsilon w_\gamma(\varepsilon)=a\,\varepsilon^{-1}+b\log\varepsilon .
Proof.

$\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\big(w_\gamma-a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\log\varepsilon\big)=\varepsilon^{-1}\big(\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}w_\gamma+a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\big)=\varepsilon^{-1}O(\varepsilon)$ is bounded near $\varepsilon=0$, so $w_\gamma-a\varepsilon^{-1}-b\log\varepsilon$ has a limit and differs from it by $O(\varepsilon)$. ∎

Lemma 5.5 (Gaussian integral over the loop momentum).
Let $t_1,t_2>0$, $p\in V$, and let the numerator be a polynomial function of $p_1\in V$ of degree at most two. Then

\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}\,e^{-t_1|p_1|^2-t_2|p_1-p|^2}\,(\text{numerator})=\frac{e^{-t_1t_2|p|^2/(t_1+t_2)}}{16\pi^2(t_1+t_2)^2}\Big[\text{numerator}-\frac{d^*d\,(\text{numerator})}{4(t_1+t_2)}\Big]_{p_1=\frac{t_2}{t_1+t_2}p},
where $d^*d$ is the positive Laplacian in the variable $p_1$. For one edge, $\int\frac{d^4p_1}{(2\pi)^4}e^{-t|p_1|^2}=(16\pi^2t^2)^{-1}$.
Proof.
Completing the square and integrating the Gaussian,

The normalised Gaussian average in the shifted variable has vanishing odd moments, and its second moment sends $(v,p_1)(v',p_1)$ to $(v,v')/(2(t_1+t_2))$ for $v,v'\in V$. A polynomial of degree at most two is its value at the centre plus a linear term plus its quadratic part; the average of the quadratic part is $\frac{1}{4(t_1+t_2)}$ times the sum of the second derivatives along an orthonormal basis, i.e. $-\frac{1}{4(t_1+t_2)}d^*d$ of the numerator. ∎

Theorem 5.12 (The quadratic counterterm).
The part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ quadratic in the fields is

The coefficient of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$ is $0$, and every quadratic local functional mixing $A|_V$ with $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, or $c$ with $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, has coefficient $0$. In terms of the ten-component field $A$,
Proof.

$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is even and of degree $0$, so by the degrees of Chapter 1 its quadratic part has legs $(A,A)$, $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*)$ or $(c,\lambda^*)$. The regulator is covariant under $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$, since $H=d^*d\otimes\mathrm{id}$ and $Q^{GF}$ commute with it, so $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is invariant. The invariant pairings of a vector of $V$ with a vector of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, of a scalar with a spinor, and of a scalar with a vector of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ vanish; this gives the vanishing mixings and the vanishing of the sectors $(c,\lambda^*)$ and $(c,A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$. The remaining sectors are the sums of the three tables, whose rows are all one-particle-irreducible one-loop graphs with these legs; the representative rows are derived in Examples [5.7](#b-00583)–[5.11](#b-00623).
