5.3 Cubic and quartic graphs

The cubic and quartic parts of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ are organised by the Weyl weights of Example [3.13](#b-00307): $A$ has weight $1$, $\lambda$ weight $\tfrac32$, $c$ weight $0$, and the antifields $A^*,\lambda^*,c^*$ the complementary weights $3,\tfrac52,4$, so that each pairing of a field with its antifield has weight $4$. The weight of a local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\cdots)$ is the sum of the weights of its fields plus the number of its derivatives, and every term of $S$ has weight $4$. The superficial degree of a graph is $4$ minus the sum of the weights of its legs: $2$ for $(A,A)$, $1$ for $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*)$, $(A|_V,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_V,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, and $0$ for the other cubic and the quartic leg sets below.
Lemma 5.14 (Weights of the singular coefficients).

Let $\gamma$ be a one-loop graph. In the expansion of its plane-wave value as $\varepsilon\to0$, the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ is a homogeneous polynomial in the leg momenta of degree equal to the superficial degree minus $2$, and the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ is homogeneous of degree equal to the superficial degree; the coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ and $\varepsilon^{-3/2}$ are homogeneous of degree equal to the superficial degree minus $1$, resp. minus $3$. Consequently, whenever these coefficients are local, the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ has weight $2$, that of $\log\varepsilon$ weight $4$, and those of $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, $\varepsilon^{-3/2}$ weights $3$, $1$.
Proof.

In momentum space, a vertex with fields of total weight $4-k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ in the momenta, since every term of $S$ has weight $4$; an edge component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ between slots of total weight $2+k$ is a polynomial of degree $k$ times $\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t_e|\text{momentum}|^2}dt_e$ (Proposition [4.10](#b-00422): degree $0$ for $A\otimes A$, $1$ for $c\otimes A^*$ and $\lambda\otimes\lambda$). Each internal half-edge contributes its weight once to a vertex and once to an edge, so the numerator of $\gamma$ is homogeneous of degree $4|V(\gamma)|-2|E(\gamma)|$ minus the sum of the weights of the legs, in the loop momentum $p_1$ and the leg momenta. Substituting $\varepsilon t_e$ for $t_e$ and $\varepsilon^{-1/2}p_1$ for $p_1$, each edge contributes a factor $\varepsilon$ and the loop measure $\varepsilon^{-2}$; with $|E(\gamma)|=|V(\gamma)|$ at one loop, the plane-wave value at scale $\varepsilon$ and leg momenta $p_j$ equals $\varepsilon$ to the power minus half the superficial degree times the plane-wave value at scale $1$ and leg momenta $\varepsilon^{1/2}p_j$. Hence, for every real $s>0$, replacing $\varepsilon$ by $s^2\varepsilon$ and every $p_j$ by $s^{-1}p_j$ multiplies the value by $s$ to the power minus the superficial degree. The singular part of an expansion in $\varepsilon^{-1/2},\varepsilon^{-1},\varepsilon^{-3/2},\log\varepsilon$ is unique, and $\log(s^2\varepsilon)-\log\varepsilon$ is finite, so each coefficient transforms separately: the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-k}$ is homogeneous of degree (superficial degree)$-2k$ and that of $\log\varepsilon$ of degree (superficial degree). The weight of a local coefficient is the sum of the leg weights, $4-$(superficial degree), plus its degree in momenta. ∎
Lemma 5.15 (Local functionals of weight at most four).

Let a local functional of degree $0$, without constant term, have weight at most $4$ and be invariant under $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ and the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$. If it is even, it is a linear combination of: in weight $2$, $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_V,A|_V)$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$; in weight $4$, functionals whose monomials have one of the field contents
where $\partial$ stands for one derivative. In weights $1$ and $3$ there are none.
Proof.

As functionals, $c$ has degree $+1$, $A^*$ and $\lambda^*$ degree $-1$, $c^*$ degree $-2$, and $A,\lambda$ degree $0$ (Chapter 1). Degree $0$ requires the number of $c$ to equal the number of $A^*$ and $\lambda^*$ plus twice the number of $c^*$, and weight at most $4$ allows at most one antifield. With $c^*$ (weight $4$): $c\,c\,c^*$. With $A^*$ (weight $3$): one $c$ and weight at most $1$ more, i.e. $c\,A^*\partial$ or $c\,A\,A^*$; invariance pairs $A^*|_V$ with $\partial$ or $A|_V$, and $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ with $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$. With $\lambda^*$ (weight $\tfrac52$): one $c$ and, by $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$, one spinor $\lambda$. Without antifields there is no $c$; the monomials are built from $A$, $\lambda$ and $\partial$, with an even number of spinors. $\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$ admits invariants of an even number of vectors of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ (the $\varepsilon$-tensor needs six) and $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)$ of an even number of vector indices from $A|_V$ and $\partial$. In weight $2$ this leaves $(A|_V)^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$; in weight $4$ the listed contents, with $A\,\partial^3$ a total derivative; in weight $1$ the single $A$, without invariant; in weight $3$ the contents $A^3$, $A\partial A$, $c\,A^*$, each with an odd number of vector indices of $V$ or of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, and $\lambda\lambda$, whose components lie in $S_+\otimes S_-$ (a vector of $V$) or in $W\otimes W$, $W^*\otimes W^*$ (without $SL(4,\mathbb C)$-invariant); all of these have vanishing invariants. ∎
Proposition 5.16 (Structure of the one-loop counterterm).

$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is the sum of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times the mass term of Theorem [5.12](#b-00630) and $\log\varepsilon$ times a local functional of weight $4$ with the field contents of Lemma [5.15](#b-00649). Its $\log\varepsilon$ part is therefore determined by the one-particle-irreducible one-loop graphs with the leg sets $(A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(\lambda,\lambda)$, $(c,A^*|_V)$, the eight cubic sets $(A|_V,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(A|_V,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_V)$, $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,A|_V,A^*|_V)$, $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,\lambda,\lambda^*)$, $(c,c,c^*)$, and the three quartic sets $(A|_V)^4$, $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$, $(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^4$.
Proof.

By Lemma [5.14](#b-00645), the coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-3/2}$, $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, $\varepsilon^{-1}$, $\log\varepsilon$ have weights $1,3,2,4$; by invariance of the regulator and Lemma [5.15](#b-00649), the first two vanish, the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ is a combination of the two mass terms, computed in Theorem [5.12](#b-00630), and the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ has the listed contents. The coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-2}$ has weight $0$ and is a constant. ∎
5.3.1 Cubic graphs

Every cubic graph below has vanishing coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$, in accordance with Lemma [5.14](#b-00645). Its $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient, as a multilinear form in the three legs, is a rational multiple of the tree vertex function of Definition [2.12](#b-00156) with the same legs; the tables give these multiples, in units of $\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$. 5.3.2 Quartic graphs

For the quartic sets leg $j\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ carries a decomposable fibre element $(v_j,-)\otimes X_j$ with $X_j\in\mathfrak g$, $v_j\in V$ for a leg $A|_V$ and $v_j\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ for a leg $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$; in the set $(A|_V)^2(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})^2$ legs $1,2$ are $A|_V$ and legs $3,4$ are $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$. A multilinear form is determined by its values on such legs, and by Lemma [5.14](#b-00645) the $\log\varepsilon$ coefficients are independent of the momenta. They are written in the basis of products of a colour factor and a Lorentz factor:

• colour factors: the pairing $([X_1,X_2],[X_3,X_4])$ of the bracket of the colour elements of legs $1,2$ with the bracket of those of legs $3,4$; the pairing $([X_1,X_4],[X_2,X_3])$; and the averaged trace $\tfrac1{24}\sum_{\text{orderings}}\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2}\mathrm{ad}_{X_3}\mathrm{ad}_{X_4})$, the fourth-order adjoint trace averaged over the $24$ orderings of $X_1,\dots,X_4$. The third pairing $([X_1,X_3],[X_2,X_4])$ is the sum of the first two, by the Jacobi identity and the invariance of $(-,-)$.
• Lorentz factors: $(v_1,v_2)(v_3,v_4)$, $(v_1,v_3)(v_2,v_4)$, $(v_1,v_4)(v_2,v_3)$, products of metric pairings.

5.3.3 The logarithmic part as a rescaling of the fields

Write $\int(A,A^*)$, $\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)$, $\int(c^*,c)$ for the local functionals $e\mapsto\langle e_A,e_{A^*}\rangle$, $\langle e_{\lambda^*},e_\lambda\rangle$, $\langle e_{c^*},e_c\rangle$, the pairing of Definition [2.5](#b-00091) applied to the components of the field $e$ in the two slots of a pair, the even member first; the first uses all ten components of $A$. For a monomial in the fields, let $n_A,n_{A^*},n_\lambda,n_{\lambda^*},n_c,n_{c^*}$ denote the numbers of its factors of each kind.
Lemma 5.17 (The bracket as a field count).
For every monomial $F$ in the fields,
\Big\{\int(A,A^*),F\Big\}=(n_A-n_{A^*})F,\qquad \Big\{\int(\lambda^*,\lambda),F\Big\}=(n_{\lambda^*}-n_\lambda)F,\qquad \Big\{\int(c^*,c),F\Big\}=(n_{c^*}-n_c)F .
Hence, on every monomial of $S$,
\Big\{2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c),\,F\Big\}=\big(2(n_A-n_{A^*})+4(n_\lambda-n_{\lambda^*})+(n_c-n_{c^*})\big)F .
Proof.

By Definition [2.6](#b-00095), the kernel $K_0$ pairs each even member $A,\lambda^*,c^*$ with its odd partner $A^*,\lambda,c$ with the coefficient $-\delta(x-y)$ times the inverse fibre pairing, which is the structure $K_0=-\sum(x_i\otimes\xi_i+\xi_i\otimes x_i)$, $\Delta_0=\sum\partial_{x_i}\partial_{\xi_i}$ of [C07, §10.1] for an even coordinate $x_i$ and its odd partner $\xi_i$, applied pointwise. For one pair, $x_i\xi_i$ is odd, and

The bracket with a fixed functional is a derivation, because $\Delta_0$ is a second-order operator, so $\{x_i\xi_i,-\}=x_i\partial_{x_i}-\xi_i\partial_{\xi_i}$ counts $x_i$ minus $\xi_i$. The three functionals of the lemma are the sums of $x_i\xi_i$ over the components, with $x_i$ the even member, which gives the three identities; the combination follows by linearity. ∎
Theorem 5.18 (The logarithmic part of the one-loop counterterm).
The $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is
\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\,\log\varepsilon\,\big(Q+\{I,-\}\big)\Big(2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c)\Big). \tag{5.6}

Equivalently, it multiplies each monomial of $S$ by $2(n_A-n_{A^*})+4(n_\lambda-n_{\lambda^*})+(n_c-n_{c^*})$: the bracket acts as a weighted field count with weights $2$ for $A$, $4$ for $\lambda$, $1$ for $c$, and the opposite weights for the antifields.
Proof.
The functional $2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c)$ is odd. By Proposition [2.11](#b-00133), $Q$ applied to it equals its bracket with $\tfrac12\langle e,Qe\rangle$, so
by the graded symmetry of Definition [2.6](#b-00095), $S$ being even. By Lemma [5.17](#b-00719), this bracket multiplies the terms of $S$ by

These are the computed multiples: the quadratic ones by Theorem [5.12](#b-00630) and Remark [5.13](#b-00639) (with the coefficient $0$ of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$, absent from $S$), the cubic ones $6,6,10,10,1,1,1,1$ by the totals of the eight cubic tables, and the quartic ones $8,8,8$ by the totals of the three quartic tables. In the cubic and quartic sets the computed coefficient equals the multiple of the tree vertex as a multilinear form, including the two chirality structures of $(\lambda,\lambda,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ and of $(c,\lambda,\lambda^*)$. By Proposition [5.16](#b-00655) these leg sets carry the whole $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, so the two local functionals coincide. ∎
Corollary 5.19 (The coupling counterterm vanishes at one loop).

Suppose the $\log\varepsilon$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is written as $\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\log\varepsilon$ times the sum of $\{S,-\}$ of an element of the span of $\int(A|_V,A^*|_V)$, $\int(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $\int(c^*,c)$ and the two chiral parts of $\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)$, and a multiple of $S$. Then the multiple of $S$ is $0$ and the element is $2\int(A,A^*)-4\int(\lambda^*,\lambda)-\int(c^*,c)$. The same holds with $S$ replaced by its classical part, the terms of $S$ without antifields. Since the coupling constant sits in $(-,-)$ and enters $S$ as an overall factor, the one-loop $\log\varepsilon$ counterterm is a rescaling of the fields with vanishing component along the coupling.
Proof.

By Lemma [5.17](#b-00719), $\{S,-\}$ of an element of the span multiplies each monomial of $S$ by a sum of field counts weighted by the coefficients of the element, additive over the factors of the monomial, and a multiple of $S$ adds the same number to every monomial. The terms of $S$ built from $A|_V$ alone contain $2$, $3$, $4$ factors $A|_V$, with computed multiples $4$, $6$, $8$: an additive weight times $2,3,4$ plus a common constant fits $4,6,8$ with weight $2$ and constant $3\cdot4-2\cdot6=0$. With the constant $0$: the kinetic terms of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ and $\lambda$ give the weight $2$ of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ and the sum $8$ of the two chiral weights of $\lambda$; the vertex $\lambda\lambda A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, whose two structures have both $\lambda$ of the same chirality, gives each chiral weight $(10-2)/2=4$; the ghost kinetic term $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A^*)$ gives the weight $-1+2=1$ of $c$; the remaining eight multiples are then reproduced. For the classical part: by Lemma [5.17](#b-00719) every term of $S$ containing an antifield has $n_c-n_{c^*}=1$ and every classical term has $n_c=n_{c^*}=0$, so $S$ minus its classical part equals $\{S,-\int(c^*,c)\}$, an element of the span; replacing $S$ by its classical part shifts the element by a multiple of $\int(c^*,c)$ and leaves the multiple unchanged. ∎
Remark 5.20 (The mass term has nonzero BV variation).

The $\varepsilon^{-1}$ part of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, the mass term $\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\tfrac94\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$, has nonzero variation under $Q+\{I,-\}$. Indeed $\{I,\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)\}$ pairs the $A^*$ of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$ with $A$ and is a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A)=-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(c,[A,A])=0$, the bracket $[A,A]$ contracting the symmetric metric with the antisymmetric bracket of $\mathfrak g$. By Proposition [2.11](#b-00133), $Q$ inserts $Qc=-dc$ into the slot of $A|_V$, so

\big(Q+\{I,-\}\big)\Big(\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\tfrac94\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)\Big)=-\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\tfrac92\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V).
This is the breaking of the gauge symmetry by the regulator. The next section shows how the master equation at the UV boundary absorbs it and what it leaves behind.
5.4 The quantum master equation at the UV boundary
Definition 5.21 (Defect vertex).
For an even functional $J$ with values in $\mathbb C[[\hbar]]$, at least cubic modulo $\hbar$, the defect vertex at scale $\varepsilon$ is the odd functional
D_\varepsilon=QJ+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J,
with $\Delta_\varepsilon$ and $\{-,-\}_\varepsilon$ of Definition [4.13](#b-00445). By Corollary [4.15](#b-00460), $D_\varepsilon=0$ is the quantum master equation at scale $\varepsilon$.
Proposition 5.22 (The $Q$-variation at scale $\infty$ is the flow of the defect).
Let $\delta$ be an odd parameter with $\delta^2=0$ [C07, (12.0.1)]. On functionals without superconformal ghosts,
Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J+\delta D_\varepsilon). \tag{5.7}

Thus $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)$ is the sum of the connected graphs with exactly one vertex labelled by $D_\varepsilon$, all other vertices by $J$, and all edges by $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ [C07, §15.4].
Proof.

For an even $J$, the product rule of Definition [4.13](#b-00445) gives $(Q+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon)e^{J/\hbar}=\hbar^{-1}D_\varepsilon\,e^{J/\hbar}$, as in the proof of Corollary [4.15](#b-00460). Since $\delta D_\varepsilon$ is even and $\delta^2=0$, $e^{(J+\delta D_\varepsilon)/\hbar}=e^{J/\hbar}\big(1+\hbar^{-1}\delta D_\varepsilon\big)$, so $\hbar^{-1}D_\varepsilon e^{J/\hbar}=\partial_\delta e^{(J+\delta D_\varepsilon)/\hbar}$. Theorem [4.14](#b-00448) without superconformal ghosts and the fact that $\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}$ is independent of $\delta$ give
The left side is $\hbar^{-1}\big(Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)\big)e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}$, $Q$ being a derivation. On the right,
W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J+\delta D_\varepsilon)=W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)+\delta\,\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J+\delta D_\varepsilon),

so the right side is $\hbar^{-1}\big(\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J+\delta D_\varepsilon)\big)e^{W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}$. The graph statement is Proposition [4.20](#b-00495) applied to $J+\delta D_\varepsilon$, keeping the terms linear in $\delta$. ∎

With $\Delta_\infty=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$, the quantum master equation at scale $\infty$ for the renormalised flow is $Q\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)=0$ (Corollary [4.15](#b-00460)). Its failure at order $\hbar$ is the one-loop obstruction, the order-$\hbar$ part of $\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$, which is the form taken by the obstruction of [C07, Prop 12.0.3] with the upper scale at $\infty$; by [(5.7)](#b-00753) it is a sum of graphs with one defect vertex.
Proposition 5.23 (The defect vertex at one loop).
For $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, with $I$ the classical interaction [(2.3)](#b-00153),
D_\varepsilon=\tfrac12\big(\{I,I\}_\varepsilon-\{I,I\}\big)+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon I-Q\,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon+(\text{terms of order }\hbar^2). \tag{5.8}
The first term is the bracket built from $\Delta_\varepsilon-\Delta_0=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon-K_0}$, i.e. two vertices of $I$ joined by one special edge carrying
K_\varepsilon-K_0=-\int_0^\varepsilon(H\otimes1)K_t\,dt,
which in momentum space is $e^{-\varepsilon|p|^2}-1$ times the components of $K_0$; its Schwinger time lies in $[0,\varepsilon]$.
Proof.

Expanding $D_\varepsilon$ with $J=I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ of order $\hbar$: at order $\hbar^0$, $QI+\tfrac12\{I,I\}_\varepsilon$; at order $\hbar$, $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]-\tfrac12\big(\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon+\{I^{CT}[\varepsilon],I\}_\varepsilon\big)+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon I$, where the two brackets of even functionals coincide; the rest is $\tfrac12\{I^{CT}[\varepsilon],I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon-\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, of order $\hbar^2$. The classical master equation (Proposition [2.13](#b-00167)) gives $QI=-\tfrac12\{I,I\}$, with $\{-,-\}$ built from $\Delta_0$ (Definition [2.6](#b-00095)). From $K_t=(e^{-tH}\otimes1)K_0$, $\frac{d}{dt}K_t=-(H\otimes1)K_t$, and integration from $0$ to $\varepsilon$ gives the special edge; in momentum space $e^{-tH}$ is $e^{-t|p|^2}$. ∎

At order $\hbar$, the graphs of [(5.7)](#b-00753) with two legs are: the term $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ as a vertex; the bubbles formed by the two vertices of $\tfrac12(\{I,I\}_\varepsilon-\{I,I\})$, joined by the special edge and one edge $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$; and one-particle-reducible graphs in which a loop closes at a single cubic vertex. The term $\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$ has at least three legs.
Lemma 5.24 (Two-leg sectors of degree one).

An invariant local functional of degree $1$ with two legs and weight at most $4$ is a combination of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$ (weight $2$) and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$ (weight $4$). In particular the sectors with legs $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ and $(c,\lambda)$ vanish.
Proof.

Degree $1$ with two legs requires one $c$ and one leg of degree $0$, $A$ or $\lambda$. The invariant pairings of a scalar with a spinor and with a vector of $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ vanish. With $A|_V$: one derivative in weight $2$, $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$; three derivatives in weight $4$, where $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,d^*dA|_V)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d\,dc,dA|_V)=0$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,dd^*A|_V)=\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$. ∎

blocks.source: Lemma 5.25 (Graphs with one special edge).

The plane-wave value of each bubble of the first figure is $\varepsilon^{-1}$ times a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$ plus a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$ plus $O(\varepsilon)$, with vanishing coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$.
Proof.

The special edge carries $-\int_0^\varepsilon(\cdots)e^{-t_1|p_1|^2}dt_1$ and the other edge $\int_\varepsilon^\infty(\cdots)e^{-t_2|p_1-p|^2}dt_2$. After the Gaussian integral over $p_1$ (Lemma [5.5](#b-00548), extended to the polynomial numerators of degree three of these graphs by the same moments), the integrand is $(t_1+t_2)^{-2}e^{-t_1t_2|p|^2/(t_1+t_2)}$ times a sum of terms $(t_1+t_2)^{-m}$, $m\ge0$, with polynomial coefficients in $\frac{t_1}{t_1+t_2}$ and $p$. On $[0,\varepsilon]\times[\varepsilon,\infty)$ the exponent satisfies $0\le\frac{t_1t_2|p|^2}{t_1+t_2}\le t_1|p|^2\le\varepsilon|p|^2$, so its exponential is a power series in $\varepsilon|p|^2$ with uniform remainders. Substituting $\varepsilon t_1$, $\varepsilon t_2$ for $t_1$, $t_2$ maps the region to $[0,1]\times[1,\infty)$, on which $(t_1+t_2)^{-2-m}$ is integrable, and each term becomes an integer power of $\varepsilon$ times a convergent integral. Hence the value is a series in integer powers of $\varepsilon$; by Lemma [5.24](#b-00771) the coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\varepsilon^0$ are the two listed functionals. ∎

The one-loop part of $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ with legs $(c,A|_V)$, graph by graph, in units of $\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(16\pi^2(X,Y))$. Theorem 5.26 (The one-loop obstruction in the sector $(c,A|_V)$).

The part of $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ of order $\hbar$ with legs $(c,A|_V)$ has the following $\varepsilon$-expansion: the special-edge bubbles contribute $-\tfrac92\,\varepsilon^{-1}$ times $\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$, the vertex $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ contributes $+\tfrac92\,\varepsilon^{-1}$ times the same functional, the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$ is $0$, and the limit is

-\frac{27}{8}\,\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)=\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\;Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V). \tag{5.9}
The sectors $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ and $(c,\lambda)$ of the one-loop obstruction vanish.
Proof.

By Proposition [5.22](#b-00751) and [(5.8)](#b-00764), the order-$\hbar$ part with two legs is the sum of the graphs listed before Lemma [5.24](#b-00771). The one-particle-reducible graphs vanish: a loop closing at one cubic vertex contracts two legs of a vertex of the form $([X,Y],Z)$ with $(-,-)^{-1}$ and gives $\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X)=0$ or the contraction of the antisymmetric bracket with the symmetric $(-,-)^{-1}$, both zero. The same argument gives $\Delta_\varepsilon I=0$: $K_\varepsilon$ pairs a field with its antifield, the vertices of $I$ containing an antifield are $([A,c],A^*)$, $([c,\lambda],\lambda^*)$, $\tfrac12([c,c],c^*)$, and each self-contraction is a trace of $\mathrm{ad}$. The five bubbles are given in the table; their $\varepsilon^{-1}$ coefficients sum to $-\tfrac94+\tfrac18-\tfrac92+2+\tfrac18=-\tfrac92$, and by Lemma [5.25](#b-00777) they have vanishing $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient. By Theorem [5.12](#b-00630) and Remark [5.20](#b-00742), $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ restricted to $(c,A|_V)$ is $-\tfrac94\cdot(-2)=\tfrac92$ times $\varepsilon^{-1}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A|_V)$ in the unit; its $\log\varepsilon$ part restricted to $(c,A|_V)$ vanishes, because $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)$ contains $d\,dc=0$, $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,A^*)$ restricted to $(c,A|_V)$ is $-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dc,d^*dA|_V)=-\tfrac12\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d\,dc,dA|_V)=0$, and the coefficient of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$ is $0$. The finite parts sum to $-\tfrac58-\tfrac1{12}-\tfrac54-\tfrac43-\tfrac1{12}=-\tfrac{81}{24}=-\tfrac{27}8$. Finally $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)=2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*(-dc))=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$, so $-\tfrac{27}8=\tfrac{27}{16}\cdot(-2)$. The last statement is Lemma [5.24](#b-00771). ∎
Remark 5.27 (The obstruction as the longitudinal part of the two-point function).

$Q$ preserves the polynomial degree of functionals, so the part of $Q\,W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ with legs $(c,A|_V)$ at order $\hbar$ is $Q$ applied to the order-$\hbar$ quadratic part of $W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon])$: the renormalised two-point function, whose limit as $\varepsilon\to0$ exists by Theorem [5.12](#b-00630). $Q$ annihilates its $(c,A^*)$ part on $(c,A|_V)$, since $\iota_p$ of $|p|^2A|_V-p\,\iota_pA|_V$ is $0$, and its transverse $A|_V$ part, which depends on $A|_V$ through $dA|_V$. Hence the cancellation of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and the vanishing of $\log\varepsilon$ in Theorem [5.26](#b-00783) follow from Theorem [5.12](#b-00630), and the obstruction is $Q$ of the longitudinal part of the renormalised $A|_V$ two-point function at scale $\infty$. A longitudinal quadratic functional of $A|_V$ is $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,G\,d^*A|_V)$ for a translation-invariant operator $G$ on functions, and $Q$ sends it to $-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,G\,d^*A|_V)$; comparing with [(5.9)](#b-00785) shows that $G$ is the constant $\tfrac{27}{16}$ in the unit, so the longitudinal part is the local functional
\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V).

A direct evaluation of the longitudinal parts of the graphs of the $A|_V$ two-point function, with every edge cut off at $\varepsilon$, reproduces $-\tfrac92\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $-\tfrac{27}8$; there the gauge bubble and the ghost loop carry separate $\log(\varepsilon|p|^2)$ and $\log2$ terms in their longitudinal parts, which cancel in their sum. Theorem [5.26](#b-00783) is the evaluation of the same quantity through the UV-boundary identity, on graphs with one special edge confined to $[0,\varepsilon]$.
Theorem 5.28 (The finite counterterm in the sector $(c,A|_V)$).
Replace the renormalised interaction $I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ by
I-\frac{27}{16}\,\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]. \tag{5.10}

Then $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ at one loop is unchanged, the limit of the flow exists, and the part with legs $(c,A|_V)$ of the one-loop obstruction vanishes. The added term is local, even, of degree $0$ and weight $4$, independent of $\varepsilon$, and invariant under translations, $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$, the adjoint action of $\mathfrak g$ and the dilatation. Among the quadratic functionals of $A|_V$ of weight $4$ and degree $0$, it is unique up to adding multiples of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA|_V,dA|_V)$, which is $Q$-closed.
Proof.

The added term is of order $\hbar$, so at order $\hbar$ it enters the flow as a tree vertex, with a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$, and leaves the one-loop singular parts unchanged. In [(5.8)](#b-00764) it adds $-Q$ of itself at order $\hbar$, and $-\{I,\cdot\}_\varepsilon$ of itself, which has at least three legs. By Theorem [5.26](#b-00783) and $Q\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)=-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)$, the $(c,A|_V)$ part becomes $-\tfrac{27}{8}+\tfrac{27}{16}\cdot2=0$ in the unit. Invariance under the dilatation holds because the weight is $4$. For uniqueness: by Lemma [5.15](#b-00649), the quadratic functionals of $A|_V$ of weight $4$ are spanned by $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA|_V,dA|_V)$ and $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$; the first is $Q$-closed, since $d\,dc=0$, and the second has $Q$-variation $-2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*dc,d^*A|_V)\neq0$, so the coefficient $\tfrac{27}{16}$ of the second is forced. ∎
Remark 5.29 (Renormalisation conditions belong to the definition of the theory).

$I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is unique and purely singular [C07, Thm B]; the finite term of [(5.10)](#b-00795) is a finite change of the interaction, $I\mapsto I-\tfrac{27}{16}\frac{\hbar\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$, of the kind that lifts a theory across a $Q$-exact obstruction in [C07, Lemma 12.0.4]. The regulated theory with $I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ has a finite limit and fails the master equation at scale $\infty$ by a finite local amount; the master equation forces the coefficient $\tfrac{27}{16}$ and leaves the $Q$-closed finite counterterms, such as multiples of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(dA,dA)$, free. This choice is a renormalisation condition, and it is part of the definition of the quantum theory: every observable $O[\infty]$ is built from the flow of the interaction, and changes with it. In this program it is the first instance of that statement; the same mechanism recurs for the equivariant counterterms of the superconformal ghosts.
Remark 5.30 (The cubic sector of the obstruction).

The one-loop obstruction also has components with three legs: $(c,A|_V,A|_V)$, $(c,A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$, $(c,\lambda,\lambda)$ and $(c,c,A^*|_V)$. They are sums of triangles and quartic-vertex bubbles with one special edge, of the vertex $-\{I,I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\}_\varepsilon$, and of one-particle-reducible graphs in which $-QI^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is joined to $I$ by an edge $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$. The finite term of [(5.10)](#b-00795) changes them by $-\{I,\cdot\}$ of itself, a nonzero functional built from $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,([A,c],A^*)$. The full one-loop master equation, i.e. the vanishing of the obstruction in all sectors after a finite counterterm, is the subject of Step 2.
Proposition 5.31 (The finite counterterm under special conformal transformations).

Let $v$ be the special conformal field $x\mapsto(x,x)v_1-2(v_1,x)x$, $v_1\in V$ (Definition [3.1](#b-00188)), acting on $A|_V$ by the Lie derivative $L_v$ (Definition [3.12](#b-00297)). The derivative of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*A|_V)$ along $A|_V\mapsto L_vA|_V$ is
2\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,d^*L_vA|_V)=-8\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(d^*A|_V,\iota_{v_1}A|_V)\neq0,
while for translations, rotations and the dilatation $2E$ the derivative vanishes.
Proof.

For a conformal Killing field $v$ of $V$, the symmetric part of the derivative of $(v,-)$ is $\tfrac14\operatorname{div}v$ times the metric; taking one more divergence, $d^*d$ applied to the components of $v$ is $\tfrac12\operatorname{grad}(\operatorname{div}v)$. The Lie derivative of the one-form $A|_V$ is $v(A|_V)+A|_V\circ(\text{derivative of }v)$, and the divergence of this expression, with the two identities above, is
d^*(L_vA|_V)=v(d^*A|_V)+\tfrac12(\operatorname{div}v)\,d^*A|_V+\tfrac12\,\iota_{\operatorname{grad}(\operatorname{div}v)}A|_V .
Hence

and integration by parts cancels the first two terms, since $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,v(\cdot)=-\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\operatorname{div}v)(\cdot)$. For the special conformal field, $\operatorname{div}v=-8(v_1,x)$ (Chapter 2) and $\operatorname{grad}(\operatorname{div}v)=-8v_1$, which gives the stated value. For translations and rotations $\operatorname{div}v=0$, and for $2E$, $\operatorname{div}v=8$ is constant. ∎

The finite counterterm of Theorem [5.28](#b-00793) is the Feynman-gauge longitudinal term, and Proposition [5.31](#b-00803) shows that it breaks the special conformal symmetry. In Step 2 the components of the equivariant counterterms along the special conformal generators have to absorb this variation, or exhibit it as part of an obstruction.
Remark 5.32 (Method of computation).

Each per-graph coefficient of this chapter was computed in an explicit realisation of $V_{10}$, $\Sigma$ and $\mathfrak g$, with the loop momentum integrated exactly as a Gaussian (Lemma [5.5](#b-00548)) and the $\varepsilon$-expansion taken exactly on the graphs with one pinned edge (Proposition [5.3](#b-00532)), in exact rational arithmetic over $\mathbb Q(i)$, and every graph was evaluated a second time independently, with identical results; for the two-point graphs the second evaluation used floating-point arithmetic with rational reconstruction. For the two-point graphs the polarisations and momenta were symbolic. For the cubic and quartic sets, each multilinear form was determined by exact linear algebra on a basis of the $\mathrm{Spin}(4,\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{Spin}(6,\mathbb C)$-invariant multilinear forms of the given legs, including the parity-odd ones, from evaluations at integer polarisations and momenta drawn at random; the sampled configurations outnumber the basis, the linear system has full rank, and the solution agrees exactly with every further sample. A nonzero polynomial vanishes at a point whose coordinates are drawn independently and uniformly from a finite set of integers with probability at most its total degree divided by the size of the set (Schwartz–Zippel); random integer samples therefore give a full-rank system with high probability, full rank is then checked exactly, and the resulting coefficients are exact. The colour factors were reduced exactly for a general simple $\mathfrak g$ in one evaluation and for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(2)$ in the other; the purely bosonic graphs and the sector $(c,A|_V)$ of the obstruction were evaluated a third time, the latter through the renormalised two-point function of Remark [5.27](#b-00789).
6. Local operators: from functionals to local $O(\varepsilon)$

The insertion of a composite operator into a one-loop graph diverges as $\varepsilon\to0$, and Costello's construction asks for a family $O(\varepsilon)$ whose flow to scale $\infty$ has a limit. At scale $\infty$, however, $K_\infty=0$ and $P(0,\infty)$ is a contracting homotopy for $Q$ on decaying sections (Chapter 3), so a general functional family $O(\varepsilon)$ produces a class that is fixed by the finitely many zero-mode classes alone. The content of an operator is therefore the requirement that $O(\varepsilon)$ be local, $O(\varepsilon)=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ with coefficients in $\mathrm{span}\{\varepsilon^{-1},\log\varepsilon\}$: locality and the existence of the limit fix the singular part, and the finite part is the scheme. This chapter sets up $O(\varepsilon)$ and $O[\infty]$, proves $O(\varepsilon)=O$ for single letters at one loop, and computes $O(\varepsilon)$ for the scalar bilinears graph by graph.
6.1 Observables as first-order deformations
Definition 6.1 (Background field and the family $I+\delta O$).
A background field is a compactly supported four-form $\omega\in\Omega^4_c(\mathbb R^4)$ [CG2, Lemma 10.1.1.3]. A local operator is a local functional
O=\int\omega\,(\text{density}),

linear in $\omega$, whose density is a polynomial in the fields and their derivatives at a point; the Weyl weight $w_O$ of $O$ is the sum of the Weyl weights of the fields in the density ($c$: $0$, $A$: $1$, $\lambda$: $\tfrac32$, $A^*$: $3$, $\lambda^*$: $\tfrac52$, $c^*$: $4$) plus the number of derivatives. For $O$ of cohomological degree $i$, $\delta$ is a square-zero parameter of degree $-i$ [CG2, Def 8.3.1.1], and $I+\delta O$ is a family of interactions over $\mathbb C[\delta]/\delta^2$; by [CG2, after Def 8.3.1.3] it satisfies the axioms of a family of theories over $\mathbb C[\delta]/\delta^2$ except locality of the flowed functionals. All operators of this chapter have $i=0$.
The square-zero parameter $\delta$ is written without argument; the delta distribution is always written with its argument, as in $\delta(x-y)$.
Definition 6.2 (The local family and the observable at scale $\infty$).

Let $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ be the one-loop counterterm of $I$ [C07, Thm B] (Definition [5.1](#b-00525)), and write the counterterm of the family $I+\delta O$ as $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$. Put

O(\varepsilon):=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon],\qquad O[\infty]:=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big), \tag{6.1}

with $W$ the flow of Definition [4.19](#b-00491) [CG2, §7.2.7]. With the global ghosts of $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$, $I$ is replaced by the equivariant interaction $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}=I+S^{(1)}+S^{(2)}$ [ESW, Rem 1.29] (Definition [3.10](#b-00269)) and $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ by the counterterm of the family $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}+\delta O$ over $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))$:

O(\varepsilon):=O-\partial_\delta I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon],\qquad O[\infty]:=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),\,I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}-I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,O(\varepsilon)\big).

Both are cochains on $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$; their components of arity $0$ are the functionals [(6.1)](#b-00826). This chapter computes the components of arity $0$; the components with arguments in $\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)$ involve the counterterms of $I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}$ along the ghosts and are taken up in Chapter 6.
At scale $\infty$ the differential on observables is $(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]$, since $\Delta_\infty=0$ and $\{-,-\}_\infty=0$ (Definition [4.13](#b-00445)) [CG2, Def 8.3.1.3, Prop 13.4.0.1].
[C07, Thm B] is stated for interactions that are at least cubic modulo $\hbar$, and $\delta O$ is quadratic for the operators below. The construction of [C07, Thm B] is applied graph by graph:
Proposition 6.3 (Counterterms of the family).

Let $O$ be a local operator of degree $0$. At order $\hbar$ there is a unique local functional $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]\in\mathscr O_l(\mathscr E)\otimes\mathscr A_{<0}$, with $\mathscr A_{<0}=\mathrm{span}\{\varepsilon^{-1},\log\varepsilon\}$ [C07, Def 8.0.2; CG2, §13.7.2], such that the limit [(6.1)](#b-00826) exists. It is the singular part of the sum of the one-loop graphs in which the vertex $O$ lies on the cycle, each evaluated with $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$.
Proof.

By Proposition [4.20](#b-00495), the order-$\hbar$ part of $\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta O)$ is a sum over connected graphs with exactly one vertex $O$ (since $\delta^2=0$) and either one cycle and vertices $I$, or no cycle and one vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$. Every vertex of $I$ is at least trivalent and $O$ occurs once, so for a fixed number of legs the sum is finite. Three classes occur.

• $O$ lies off the cycle. Removing the edges that join $O$ to the rest leaves a one-loop graph without $O$; the corresponding tree graph with the vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in its place cancels its singular part by [C07, Thm B] for $I$ (Remark [5.2](#b-00529)), and the trees joining $O$ converge to trees with $P(0,\infty)$, because $P(\varepsilon,\infty)-P(0,\infty)=-\int_0^\varepsilon L_t\,dt$ is of order $\varepsilon$ at fixed nonzero momentum.

• $O$ lies on the cycle. The singular part of such a graph is a local functional (computed explicitly below for every operator of this chapter), and the tree with the vertex $-\delta\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ in place of the cycle removes it.
• Trees with the vertex $-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and with $O$: already paired in the first class.

Uniqueness: two such counterterms differ by a local functional $X(\varepsilon)$ with values in $\mathscr A_{<0}$ whose tree-level flow has a limit. The part of the tree-level flow of $X(\varepsilon)$ with as many legs as $X(\varepsilon)$ is $X(\varepsilon)$ itself, so $X(\varepsilon)$ has a limit, and its singular part vanishes. ∎
Proposition 6.4 (Local representatives).
Let $O$ be a local operator of degree $0$.
• Two local families $O(\varepsilon)$, $O^{\prime}(\varepsilon)$ for which the limit [(6.1)](#b-00826) exists have the same singular part.
• For an $\varepsilon$-independent local functional $X$ of order $\hbar$, the family $O(\varepsilon)+X$ gives the observable $O[\infty]+X[\infty]$.

• Let $F$ be a functional of decaying sections, without constant term, with $QF=0$. Then $F$ is $Q$-exact up to the finitely many zero-mode classes of Theorem [4.16](#b-00469) (Corollary [4.17](#b-00480)).
Consequently a statement about $O[\infty]$ has content when it is written in the form
(d_{CE}+Q)\,O[\infty]=(\text{a local functional})[\infty],
and an anomalous dimension is a class in the cohomology of local functionals.
Proof.

The first item is the uniqueness part of Proposition [6.3](#b-00832). The second follows from linearity of [(6.1)](#b-00826) in the $\delta$-component, at order $\hbar$, where $X$ enters through its tree-level flow. The third item is Corollary [4.17](#b-00480), which rests on the homotopy identity $Q\,P(0,\infty)\star+P(0,\infty)\star\,Q=\mathrm{id}$ of Theorem [4.16](#b-00469) on decaying sections, with the zero-mode classes listed there. Every observable $O[\infty]$ of degree $0$ with $(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]=0$ therefore lies, up to these classes, in the image of $Q$ on functionals; the class it represents is recorded by the local functional $O(\varepsilon)$ through the first two items. ∎
Remark 6.5 (Where the content of an operator lies).

By Proposition [6.4](#b-00840), the singular part of $O(\varepsilon)$ is uniquely fixed and the finite part is the scheme freedom; this is the statement of Remark [4.18](#b-00488) for operators. In the rest of this chapter $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ is computed; its $\log\varepsilon$ part is the input of the anomalous dimensions in Chapter 6.
6.2 Tools for one-loop insertions
The gauge algebra $\mathfrak g$ is simple. The inverse pairing $(-,-)^{-1}\in\mathfrak g\otimes\mathfrak g$ is symmetric, and a bilinear form on $\mathfrak g$ can be evaluated on it.
Lemma 6.6 (Colour contractions).
For $X_1,X_2\in\mathfrak g$ and a linear map $T\colon\mathfrak g\to\mathfrak g$:
• the bracket $[-,-]$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $0$;

• the bilinear form $(-,T\,-)$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}T$; in particular $(-,-)$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $\dim\mathfrak g$, and $(X_1,[-,-])$ and $(-,[X_1,-])$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ are $0$;
• the bilinear form $([X_1,-],[X_2,-])$ evaluated on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is $-\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2})$;

• for all $X,Y\in\mathfrak g$ with $(X,Y)\neq0$, the ratio $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)/(X,Y)$ is the same number, and $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2})=\frac{\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{(X,Y)}\,(X_1,X_2)$.
Proof.

The bracket is antisymmetric and $(-,-)^{-1}$ is symmetric. The inverse pairing is characterised by the property that contracting its second factor with $(Z,-)$ returns $Z$; hence $(-,T\,-)$ on $(-,-)^{-1}$ is the trace of $T$. By invariance, $(X_1,[Z,Z^{\prime}])=([X_1,Z],Z^{\prime})=-(Z,[X_1,Z^{\prime}])$, which is $(-,T-)$ with $T=-\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$, of trace $0$ because $\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$ is antisymmetric for $(-,-)$, and $(-,[X_1,-])$ is the case $T=\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}$; and $([X_1,Z],[X_2,Z^{\prime}])=-(Z,[X_1,[X_2,Z^{\prime}]])$ is $(-,T-)$ with $T=-\mathrm{ad}_{X_1}\mathrm{ad}_{X_2}$. For simple $\mathfrak g$ every invariant symmetric bilinear form is a multiple of $(-,-)$, which gives the last item. ∎
In the following, the number
\frac{\hbar\,\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2\,(X,Y)}
is the unit of every one-loop coefficient; it is negative when $(-,-)$ is positive definite on the compact real form.
Lemma 6.7 (Vertex functions on decomposable legs).
Give each leg of a vertex a fibre element $(v,-)\otimes Z$ with $v\in V_{10}$ and $Z\in\mathfrak g$; by linearity this determines every vertex function. Then:
• the quartic vertex function [(2.5)](#b-00161) with legs $(v_j,-)\otimes Z_j$, $j=1,\dots,4$, equals
-\frac12\sum_{(ab|cd)}\big[(v_a,v_c)(v_b,v_d)-(v_a,v_d)(v_b,v_c)\big]\,\big([Z_a,Z_b],[Z_c,Z_d]\big), \tag{6.2}
the sum running over the three pairings $(12|34)$, $(13|24)$, $(14|23)$;

• the cubic vertex function [(2.4)](#b-00160) with two legs $(w,-)\otimes Z$, $(w^{\prime},-)\otimes Z^{\prime}$, $w,w^{\prime}\in W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, of incoming momenta $p$, $p^{\prime}$, and one leg $(v,-)\otimes Z^{\prime\prime}$, $v\in V$, equals
-\frac i2\,(v,p^{\prime}-p)\,(w,w^{\prime})\,\big(Z^{\prime\prime},[Z,Z^{\prime}]\big); \tag{6.3}

• the vertex function of $\int\omega\,(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ on legs $(v,-)\otimes Z$, $(v^{\prime},-)\otimes Z^{\prime}$ is $\big[(w_1,v)(w_2,v^{\prime})+(w_1,v^{\prime})(w_2,v)\big](Z,Z^{\prime})$, times the Fourier transform of $\omega$ at minus the total momentum of the legs.
Proof.

For $A_j=(v_j,-)\otimes Z_j$ the two-form $[A_a\wedge A_b]$ of Chapter 1 is $(v_a,-)\wedge(v_b,-)\otimes[Z_a,Z_b]$, because $[A_a\wedge A_b](e,e^{\prime})=(v_a,e)(v_b,e^{\prime})[Z_a,Z_b]-(v_a,e^{\prime})(v_b,e)[Z_a,Z_b]$. Polarising the normalisation of the Hodge pairing in Definition [2.8](#b-00106) gives
\big((v_a,-)\wedge(v_b,-),(v_c,-)\wedge(v_d,-)\big)=(v_a,v_c)(v_b,v_d)-(v_a,v_d)(v_b,v_c),

which gives [(6.2)](#b-00868). In [(2.4)](#b-00160), $\iota_pA(p_j)=(v_j,p)Z_j$ and $[A(p_i),A(p_j)]=(v_i,v_j)[Z_i,Z_j]$. With legs $1,2$ along $W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$ and leg $3$ along $V$, the momenta lie in $V\perp W_{\mathbb R}^\perp$, so $(v_1,p)=(v_2,p)=0$ and $(v_2,v_3)=(v_3,v_1)=0$; the second and third terms of [(2.4)](#b-00160) vanish and the first is $-\tfrac i2(v_3,p_2-p_1)(v_1,v_2)(Z_3,[Z_1,Z_2])$, which is [(6.3)](#b-00871). The last item is the multilinear part of $(\iota_{w_1}A,\iota_{w_2}A)$ on two plane waves (Definition [2.12](#b-00156)). ∎
Lemma 6.8 (Insertion on a cycle).

Expand around a background consisting of two plane waves with fibre elements $A(p_1)$, $A(p_2)$, as in Remark [4.22](#b-00517). The part of the order-$\hbar$ term of $\partial_\delta W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I+\delta O)$ that is bilinear in $A(p_1)$, $A(p_2)$ and comes from cycles through the vertex $O$ whose edges all lie in the $A$ slot is $\hbar$ times the sum of
• $\tfrac12$ times each bubble: the cycle through $O$ and one quartic vertex carrying both external legs;
• $1$ times each triangle: the cycle through $O$, a cubic vertex carrying $A(p_1)$ and a cubic vertex carrying $A(p_2)$, traversed in one orientation.

In each cycle the internal legs are contracted along the edges with the $A\otimes A$ component of $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (Proposition [4.10](#b-00422)): an edge of momentum $p$ replaces the fibre elements $(v,-)\otimes Z$, $(v^{\prime},-)\otimes Z^{\prime}$ at its two ends by $2$ times the inverse metric in $v\otimes v^{\prime}$ and $(-,-)^{-1}$ in $Z\otimes Z^{\prime}$, times $\int_\varepsilon^\infty e^{-t|p|^2}dt=e^{-\varepsilon|p|^2}|p|^{-2}$, and the loop momentum $p$ is integrated with $\int d^4p/(2\pi)^4$.
Proof.

On the $A$ slots the parity operator and the supertrace of Proposition [4.21](#b-00504) are trivial, and the one-loop operator is $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ composed with the second derivative of $I+\delta O$ in the fluctuation. The $\delta$-derivative of $\frac1{2n}\mathrm{STr}$ of its $n$-th power is $\frac12\mathrm{STr}$ of the product of $n-1$ factors built from $I$ and one factor built from $O$. The second derivative of $O$ is its vertex function with both legs internal, since $O$ is quadratic. For $n=2$ the factor built from $I$ is bilinear in the two external legs through the quartic vertex: by Definition [2.12](#b-00156) the part of the quartic term of $I$ quadratic in the fluctuation and bilinear in $A(p_1)$, $A(p_2)$ is one half of [(2.5)](#b-00161) with two internal legs, whose second derivative is [(2.5)](#b-00161) with two legs open; this gives the weight $\tfrac12$. For $n=3$ the two factors built from $I$ each carry one external leg through a cubic vertex; the two orders of these factors give equal traces, since all second derivatives and $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ are symmetric and the trace is invariant under transposition and cyclic permutation, so $\tfrac12$ times their sum is one triangle with weight $1$. ∎
The singular parts are read off from the following lemma, which also locates them on the lower end $t=\varepsilon$ of the Schwinger integrals (Remark [4.12](#b-00442)).

Proposition 6.10 (Letters).

Proof.

The vertex $O$ is univalent, and a cycle passes through every one of its vertices along two edges; hence $O$ lies off the cycle in every one-loop graph, and by Proposition [6.3](#b-00832) $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, the singular part of the graphs with $O$ on the cycle, is $0$. The graphs with $O$ off the cycle consist of a one-loop graph with the vertices of $I$, joined to $O$ by a tree. If the one-loop graph has one external leg, it is a cubic vertex of $I$ with two of its legs joined by an edge; every cubic vertex of $I$ has the form $(Z_1,[Z_2,Z_3])$ in its colour factors (Chapter 1), and joining two of its legs evaluates $(Z_1,[-,-])$ or $(-,[Z_2,-])$ on $(-,-)^{-1}$, which is $0$ by Lemma [6.6](#b-00854). All vertices of $I$ have Weyl weight $4$ (fields plus derivatives), so a one-loop graph with one vertex $O$ has superficial degree $w_O$ minus the sum of the Weyl weights of its external legs, i.e. $2$ minus that sum. Its external legs have total cohomological degree $0$; an external $c$ (weight $0$) needs an antifield (weight $\ge\frac52$) to compensate its degree, and two $\lambda$ have weight $3$. The external legs of degree $\ge0$ graphs are therefore none, one $A$, or two $A$. The element $-1$ of $SO(W_{\mathbb R}^\perp)$ lies in the image of $\mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)$ and is a symmetry of the action and of the regulator ($H$ and $Q^{GF}$ commute with $\mathrm{Spin}(6;\mathbb C)$); it fixes $w_1w_2$ and changes the sign of every functional with an odd number of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ legs, so the singular parts with one $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ leg, or with legs $A|_V$, $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, vanish. Both edges at $O$ are $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ edges. A cycle that enters a Yukawa vertex along $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ continues along $\lambda$ and needs an external $\lambda$; a cycle that enters the vertex $([A,c],A^*)$ along $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ continues along $c$ or $A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, and $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ has no $c\otimes A^*|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$ component (Proposition [4.10](#b-00422)). 7. The dilatation component and anomalous dimensions

The dilatation is the simplest superconformal component of the BV transformation of an operator. The classical theory is invariant under the rescaling of the fields by their Weyl weights, and the regulator breaks this invariance through $\varepsilon$ alone: the rescaling maps $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ to $P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty)$. Consequently the scale dependence of $O[\infty]$ is carried by the $\log\varepsilon$ parts of $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ and of $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$, and by the field-renormalisation theorem of Chapter 4 the part coming from the action is a field redefinition. This chapter proves these statements, computes the resulting coefficients for the scalar bilinears and the single letters, shows how the boundary graphs with an $L_\varepsilon$ edge produce them, and states the identification with the equivariant dilatation cochain as the task of Step 2, together with the graphs that Step 2 must evaluate.
7.1 Scaling covariance of the regulator

In $\sigma_\lambda$, $\lambda^2\varepsilon$ and $\log\lambda$ the letter $\lambda$ is a positive real number; the gaugino keeps its name $\lambda$ inside the pairings $(\lambda^*,\lambda)$ and $(\zeta,\lambda)$.
Definition 7.1 (Weyl scaling).
The Weyl weights of the slots are

slot$c$$A$$\lambda$$A^*$$\lambda^*$$c^*$
Weyl weight$0$$1$$\tfrac32$$3$$\tfrac52$$4$

For a real number $\lambda>0$ and a section $e$ in a slot of Weyl weight $w$,
(\sigma_\lambda e)(x)=\lambda^{-w}\,e(\lambda^{-1}x),

extended to $\mathscr E\otimes\mathscr E$ as $\sigma_\lambda\otimes\sigma_\lambda$ and to functionals by $(\sigma_\lambda F)(e)=F(\sigma_\lambda^{-1}e)$. For a local operator $O=\int\omega\,(\text{density})$ of Weyl weight $w_O$ (Definition [6.1](#b-00819)) we write
(E+w_O)\,O=\int\omega\,(E+w_O)(\text{density}),
where $E$ is the Euler vector field of [SW, (3)] acting on the position dependence of the density.
Lemma 7.2 (Scaling of the data).
• $\langle\sigma_\lambda e_0,\sigma_\lambda e_1\rangle=\langle e_0,e_1\rangle$ and $(\sigma_\lambda\otimes\sigma_\lambda)K_t=K_{\lambda^2t}$.

• $\sigma_\lambda Q=Q\sigma_\lambda$, $\sigma_\lambda Q^{GF}=\lambda^2Q^{GF}\sigma_\lambda$ and $\sigma_\lambda H=\lambda^2H\sigma_\lambda$; on functionals $\sigma_\lambda$ commutes with $Q$ and with the bracket.

• $\sigma_\lambda S=S$ and $\sigma_\lambda I=I$. A local functional $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$ whose density has Weyl weight $w$ (fields plus derivatives) satisfies $\sigma_\lambda\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})=\lambda^{w-4}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$; for example $\sigma_\lambda\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)=\lambda^{-2}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A,A)$.

• For a local operator $O$, $\sigma_\lambda O$ is $O$ with $\omega$ replaced by $\lambda^{w_O}$ times the pullback of $\omega$ along $x\mapsto\lambda^{-1}x$, and $\lambda\frac{d}{d\lambda}\big|_{\lambda=1}\sigma_\lambda O=(E+w_O)\,O$.
Proof.

For the pairing substitute $x=\lambda y$, $\mathrm{dvol}(x)=\lambda^4\mathrm{dvol}(y)$; the two weights add up to $4$. The scalar factor of $K_t$ (Definition [4.7](#b-00407)) becomes $\lambda^{-4}(4\pi t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4\lambda^2t}=(4\pi\lambda^2t)^{-2}e^{-|x-y|^2/4\lambda^2t}$. An operator with $j$ derivatives from a slot of weight $w$ to a slot of weight $w^{\prime}$ satisfies $\sigma_\lambda T=\lambda^{w+j-w^{\prime}}T\sigma_\lambda$. For the arrows of $Q$ (Proposition [2.11](#b-00133)) the exponent is $0+1-1$, $1+2-3$, $3+1-4$, $\tfrac32+1-\tfrac52$, all $0$; for the arrows of $Q^{GF}$ (Definition [4.1](#b-00366)) it is $3+0-1$, $1+1-0$, $4+1-3$, $\tfrac52+1-\tfrac32$, all $2$; hence also for $H=[Q,Q^{GF}]$. Every term of [(2.1)](#b-00108) has a density of Weyl weight $4$: for example $1+1+2$ for $(dA,dA)$, $\tfrac32+\tfrac32+1$ for $(\lambda,{\not d}\lambda)$, $0+1+3$ for $(dc,A^*)$ and $([A,c],A^*)$, $0+\tfrac32+\tfrac52$, $0+0+4$, and $4$ for the cubic and quartic gauge terms. For a density of weight $w$, $(\text{density})(\sigma_\lambda^{-1}e)(x)=\lambda^{w}(\text{density})(e)(\lambda x)$, and $\int\mathrm{dvol}(x)\,\lambda^w(\text{density})(\lambda x)=\lambda^{w-4}\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(\text{density})$. With $\omega$ in place of $\mathrm{dvol}$ the same substitution moves the factor $\lambda^{w_O}$ and the dilation onto $\omega$, and $\lambda\frac{d}{d\lambda}\big|_{\lambda=1}\lambda^{w_O}(\text{density})(\lambda x)=(w_O+E)(\text{density})(x)$. ∎
Proposition 7.3 (Scaling covariance).
For every $\lambda>0$ and $\varepsilon>0$,

(\sigma_\lambda\otimes\sigma_\lambda)\,P(\varepsilon,\infty)=P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty),\qquad \sigma_\lambda\,\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}=\partial_{P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty)}\,\sigma_\lambda , \tag{7.1}
and for every even functional $J$ as in Definition [4.19](#b-00491),
\sigma_\lambda\,W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J\big)=W\big(P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty),\sigma_\lambda J\big). \tag{7.2}
Proof.
By Lemma [7.2](#b-00992), $(\sigma_\lambda\otimes\sigma_\lambda)L_t=(\sigma_\lambda Q^{GF}\otimes\sigma_\lambda)K_t=\lambda^2(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_{\lambda^2t}=\lambda^2L_{\lambda^2t}$, and
(\sigma_\lambda\otimes\sigma_\lambda)\,P(\varepsilon,\infty)=\int_\varepsilon^\infty\lambda^2L_{\lambda^2t}\,dt=\int_{\lambda^2\varepsilon}^\infty L_{t}\,dt=P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty).

For linear functionals $\ell_1,\ell_2$, the operator $\partial_\phi$ of [C07, §6.4] gives $\partial_\phi\big((\ell_1\circ\sigma_\lambda^{-1})(\ell_2\circ\sigma_\lambda^{-1})\big)=(\ell_1\otimes\ell_2)\big((\sigma_\lambda^{-1}\otimes\sigma_\lambda^{-1})\phi\big)$; since $\partial_\phi$ is determined by its values on products of two linear functionals and $\sigma_\lambda$ is an even algebra automorphism of functionals, $\partial_\phi\,\sigma_\lambda=\sigma_\lambda\,\partial_{(\sigma_\lambda^{-1}\otimes\sigma_\lambda^{-1})\phi}$. With $\phi=P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty)$ and the first identity for $\lambda^{-1}$ this is the second identity in [(7.1)](#b-01001). Then $\sigma_\lambda e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{J/\hbar}=e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty)}}e^{\sigma_\lambda J/\hbar}$, and taking $\hbar\log$ gives [(7.2)](#b-01003). ∎
Lemma 7.4 (Covariance of the counterterms).

For a local family $J=I+\delta O$ with $O$ of degree $0$, let $J^{CT}[\varepsilon]=I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta\,\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ be its one-loop counterterm (Proposition [6.3](#b-00832)). Then the counterterm of the family $\sigma_\lambda J=I+\delta\,\sigma_\lambda O$ at the cutoff $\lambda^2\varepsilon$ is

(\sigma_\lambda J)^{CT}[\lambda^2\varepsilon]=\sigma_\lambda\big(J^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big)+2\log\lambda\;\sigma_\lambda\big(\text{coefficient of }\log\varepsilon\text{ in }J^{CT}[\varepsilon]\big). \tag{7.3}
In particular $\sigma_\lambda$ maps the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ in $I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ to $\lambda^{-2}$ times itself and fixes the coefficient of $\log\varepsilon$.
Proof.

At one loop $W$ is affine in the counterterm, which enters through its tree-level flow. By [(7.2)](#b-01003), $W(P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty),\sigma_\lambda J-\sigma_\lambda J^{CT}[\varepsilon])=\sigma_\lambda W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J-J^{CT}[\varepsilon])$ has a limit as $\varepsilon\to0$, and so has $W(P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty),\sigma_\lambda J-(\sigma_\lambda J)^{CT}[\lambda^2\varepsilon])$. The difference of the two counterterms is a local functional whose tree-level flow has a limit, so, as in the uniqueness part of Proposition [6.3](#b-00832), their singular parts in $\varepsilon$ coincide. Write $(\sigma_\lambda J)^{CT}[\varepsilon^{\prime}]$ as $\varepsilon^{\prime-1}$ times one local functional plus $\log\varepsilon^{\prime}$ times another. At $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\lambda^2\varepsilon$, $\log\varepsilon^{\prime}=\log\varepsilon+2\log\lambda$ and $\varepsilon^{\prime-1}=\lambda^{-2}\varepsilon^{-1}$; matching the coefficients of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ with those of $\sigma_\lambda J^{CT}[\varepsilon]$ gives [(7.3)](#b-01010), the constant $2\log\lambda$ times the $\log\varepsilon$ coefficient being the remainder. For $J=I$, $\sigma_\lambda I=I$ and uniqueness give the last statement; it agrees with Lemma [7.2](#b-00992): the coefficient of $\varepsilon^{-1}$ is a multiple of $\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_V,A|_V)+\int\mathrm{dvol}\,(A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp},A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp})$ (Theorem [5.12](#b-00630)), of density weight $2$. ∎
7.2 The Callan–Symanzik form
Definition 7.5 (Tree insertion).

For local functionals $F$ (of either parity) and $O$, the tree insertion of $F$ into $O[\infty]$ is the sum of the connected trees with one vertex $F$, one vertex $O$, any number of vertices $I$, and edges $P(0,\infty)$, with the weights of Proposition [4.20](#b-00495). For an even $F$ of order $\hbar$, at order $\hbar$ it is

\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\partial_\delta\Big[W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta O(\varepsilon)+F\big)-W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),I-I^{CT}[\varepsilon]+\delta O(\varepsilon)\big)\Big].
For a local functional $X$ of order $\hbar$, $X[\infty]$ denotes at order $\hbar$ the construction [(6.1)](#b-00826) applied to $X$: the trees with one vertex $X$ and vertices $I$.

By $\sigma_\lambda I=I$ and [(7.3)](#b-01010), with $\varepsilon^{\prime}=\lambda^2\varepsilon$,

Remark 7.10 (Reading of the three terms).

By [(7.5)](#b-01033) the action counterterm is the change of $S$ under the infinitesimal rescaling of the fields by the weights of Lemma [7.7](#b-01035); on $O[\infty]$ it acts through the bracket $\{-,O\}$ with the field-counting functional, the field redefinition proper, and through the image under $Q$ of a tree. The tree insertion of the field-counting functional into $O[\infty]$ is a nonlocal functional whose image under $Q$ is the scale-$\infty$ observable of a local functional; by Proposition [6.4](#b-00840) such terms are the ones that a statement about classes of local functionals must specify, and the identification with the equivariant dilatation cochain, stated in the last section of this chapter, specifies how this term enters. The last term involves $(Q+\{I,-\})O$ and vanishes for gauge-invariant $O$.

Remark 7.12 (The letter $A|_V$).

The letters are gauge variant, and $(Q+\{I,-\})O$ contributes. For $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_wA)$, $\int\omega\,(\zeta,\lambda)$ and $\int\omega\,(X,c)$ the linear part of $Q$ on the coordinate functional vanishes ($Q$ has no arrow into the slots of $A|_{W_{\mathbb R}^\perp}$, $\lambda$, $c$; Proposition [2.11](#b-00133)), and $(Q+\{I,-\})O=\{I,O\}$ is quadratic in the fields: the last term of [(7.8)](#b-01061) has at least two legs. For $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(A|_V))$ the arrow $c\mapsto-dc$ of $Q$ gives a linear part proportional to $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(dc))$; its tree insertion with the field-counting functional runs through the $c\otimes A^*|_V$ component of $P(0,\infty)$ (Proposition [4.10](#b-00422)) and is proportional to the longitudinal part $\int\omega\,(X,\iota_v(d(d^*d)^{-1}d^*A|_V))$. It cancels the coefficient on that part: the transverse part of $A|_V$ carries $-4$ units and the longitudinal part, which is the image of $c$ under $Q$, carries $0$.
Remark 7.13 (The Konishi value).

For $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{su}(N)$ with $(X,Y)=-\frac{4\hbar}{g^2}\operatorname{tr}(XY)$, $\operatorname{tr}$ the trace in the defining representation, $e^{S/\hbar}$ is the standard Euclidean Yang–Mills weight with coupling $g$, and $\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)=2N\operatorname{tr}(XY)$. Then
\frac{\hbar\operatorname{tr}_{\mathfrak g}(\mathrm{ad}_X\mathrm{ad}_Y)}{16\pi^2(X,Y)}=-\frac{g^2N}{32\pi^2},\qquad -24\cdot\Big(-\frac{g^2N}{32\pi^2}\Big)=\frac{3g^2N}{4\pi^2},
so the trace bilinear has dimension $2+\frac{3g^2N}{4\pi^2}$ at one loop, the one-loop value for the Konishi operator, and the twenty traceless bilinears keep dimension $2$.

By [(4.2)](#b-00437), $\lambda\frac{d}{d\lambda}\big|_{\lambda=1}P(\lambda^2\varepsilon,\infty)=2\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}P(\varepsilon,\infty)=-2\varepsilon L_\varepsilon$: the scaling acts on every edge as the boundary kernel $L_\varepsilon=(Q^{GF}\otimes1)K_\varepsilon$ at $t=\varepsilon$ (Remark [4.12](#b-00442)).
Proposition 7.15 (The coefficients on the boundary).

Let $\gamma$ be a one-loop graph whose value has the expansion $(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})\,\varepsilon^{-1}+(\log\varepsilon\text{-coefficient})\log\varepsilon+(\text{a function with a limit})$. Then

The term $2\varepsilon^{-1}(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})$ is the scaling $\lambda\frac{d}{d\lambda}\big|_{\lambda=1}$ of the counterterm $-(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})\,\varepsilon^{-1}$ under $\sigma_\lambda$ (Lemma [7.4](#b-01008)). Hence the terms $2(\cdot)$ of [(7.4)](#b-01021) are the limits of the sums of the graphs with one edge carrying $-2\varepsilon L_\varepsilon$, the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ parts cancelling against the scaling of the $\varepsilon^{-1}$ counterterms; for graphs of degree $0$ each edge carries the fraction $1/|E(\gamma)|$ (Lemma [6.9](#b-00885)).
Proof.

By Proposition [5.3](#b-00532), $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}(\text{value of }\gamma)=-\varepsilon\sum_e(\text{value with }t_e=\varepsilon)$, and $\varepsilon\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}$ of the expansion is $-(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})\varepsilon^{-1}+(\log\varepsilon\text{-coefficient})+(\text{a function tending to }0)$, the last because the finite part has an expansion in powers of $\varepsilon^{1/2}$ and $\log\varepsilon$ [C07, Def 7.1.1, Thm A]. Multiply by $2$ and add $2\varepsilon^{-1}(\varepsilon^{-1}\text{-coefficient})$. ∎

The left side of [(7.10)](#b-01079) is defined by the equivariant construction of Definition [6.2](#b-00824). By Theorem [4.14](#b-00448) and the product rule used in Corollary [4.15](#b-00460), for every even $J$ with values in $C^\bullet(\mathfrak{psl}(4|4))$,

(d_{CE}+Q)\,W\big(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J\big)=e^{-W(P(\varepsilon,\infty),J)/\hbar}\,e^{\hbar\partial_{P(\varepsilon,\infty)}}\Big(\big((d_{CE}+Q)J+\tfrac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J\big)\,e^{J/\hbar}\Big). \tag{7.11}

For $J=I_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}-I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon]+\delta O(\varepsilon)$, applying $\partial_\delta$ and $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $(d_{CE}+Q)O[\infty]$. Every bracket $\{-,-\}_\varepsilon$ and every $\Delta_\varepsilon=-\partial_{K_\varepsilon}$ is an edge carrying $K_\varepsilon$ (Remark [4.12](#b-00442)). Evaluated on $\Delta$, the component of arity one contains the vertex $S^{(1)}(\Delta)$ of Example [3.13](#b-00307), or the component of $I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon]$ along $\Delta$, exactly once. Its terms are:

• the graphs with one vertex $O(\varepsilon)$, one vertex $S^{(1)}(\Delta)$ joined by an edge $K_\varepsilon$, and edges $P(\varepsilon,\infty)$ (figure): one-loop graphs (a)–(u), and trees (v)–(y) in which the vertex is $\partial_\delta I^{CT}[\varepsilon]$;
• the graphs with the component of $I^{CT}_{\mathfrak{psl}(4|4)}[\varepsilon]$ along $\Delta$, and with the finite counterterms that the equivariant master equation requires along $\Delta$;
• the component along $\Delta$ of the equivariant master-equation defect $(d_{CE}+Q)J+\frac12\{J,J\}_\varepsilon+\hbar\Delta_\varepsilon J$ at $\delta=0$, inserted together with $O(\varepsilon)$.
